Glossary

Glossary

274 min read

Every ML term in the notes, in plain English, with its Home (the section that teaches it) and the Concept it belongs to. Each term has a fixed ID (G-118): Notes cite it right after the term, as in “learning rate (G-118)“. IDs never change; new terms take the next free number.

IDTermMeaningHomeConcept
G-11/(1−β)Roughly how many recent values a running average that favours new values (the EWMA) covers: about 10 for β=0.9.Note DL-033Exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA)
G-2465Adaptive (dynamic) decompositionCutting the state space into cells that change with the belief: small cells where the belief is high, large cells where it is near zero, as in a quadtree; it gives fine detail with far fewer cells.Note RO-015Histogram filter
G-3αThe share of confidence intervals that miss the true value they are meant to catch (the parameter). It equals one minus the confidence level.Note MA-035Confidence intervals
G-2α (Pareto shape)The number that sets how fat the tail of a Pareto distribution is (its shape parameter, also called the tail index). A larger α gives a thinner tail and fewer extreme values.Note MA-030Pareto distribution and power laws
G-2404Angle wrappingAdding or subtracting full turns until an angle or angle difference lies between −180° and 180°, so that 175° and −178° count as 7° apart, not 353°; needed whenever bearings or headings are compared.Note RO-012Concept
G-2292Angular velocity ωHow fast a robot’s heading changes, in rad/s, positive to the left; for a differential drive, the difference of the wheel speeds divided by the wheel separation.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2325atan2A function atan2(rise, run) that returns the direction of a line over the full circle from its rise and run given separately; needed because the plain inverse tangent of the ratio cannot tell opposite directions apart.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-2477Back-pointerThe note the Viterbi algorithm keeps for each state and time of which earlier state the best path came from; following them backwards from the best end recovers the most likely path.Note RO-015Hidden Markov model
G-2473Backward probability βt​The probability of the readings after time t, given state x at t, computed from the last step backwards starting at 1; it carries the evidence from the future.Note RO-015Hidden Markov model
G-2328Banana-shaped distributionThe curved cloud of end positions a motion model gives when turning noise is large: a wrong first turn sends the robot the right distance in a wrong direction, so the positions spread along an arc around the start.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-2446Bayes filterThe algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption.Note RO-014Bayes filter
G-2452Bayes’ rule with background knowledgeBayes’ theorem with an extra condition C in every term, p(x∣z,C)=p(z∣x,C) p(x∣C)/p(z∣C), such as earlier readings; it lets the posterior after one reading serve as the prior for the next.Note RO-014Bayes filter
G-2392Beam endpointThe point where a beam ends: the robot’s position plus the reading along the beam’s direction, (x+zcos(θ+θk​), y+zsin(θ+θk​)); the likelihood field model looks only at this point.Note RO-011Concept
G-2377Beam modelThe measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose.Note RO-010Concept
G-2344BearingThe angle from the robot’s heading to a sensed landmark, positive to the left, such as 86.6 degrees; together with the range it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2433BeliefThe robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, bel(xt​)=p(xt​∣z1:t​,u1:t​); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state.Note RO-013Belief
G-5βThe chance that a test misses a real effect, failing to reject a false H0​ (the probability of a Type II error). 1−β is the test’s power.Note MA-040Type I and II errors, power, tails
G-4β (beta)The number between 0 and 1 that sets how much weight a running average (the EWMA) keeps on the past; usually 0.9 in deep learning.Note DL-033Exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA)
G-6β1​, β2​Two numbers between 0 and 1 that set how much of the past Adam’s two running averages keep (its decay factors): β1​ for the average of gradients mt​, β2​ for the average of squared gradients vt​. Defaults 0.9 and 0.999.Note DL-038Adam
G-2466Binary Bayes filterThe Bayes filter for a yes-or-no state that does not change, such as “door open” or “this map cell is occupied”, run in log odds: each reading adds the log of its Bayes factor. It is fast and does not round to 0 or 1.Note RO-015Binary Bayes filter
G-7(kn​) (n choose k)The number of ways to choose k items out of n.Note MA-021Bernoulli and binomial distributions
G-2339Bitmap (obstacle bitmap)A grid of cells marked 1 if the cell contains any obstacle point and 0 otherwise, like a black-and-white image; simple and natural for sensor data, but it overstates obstacles, and finer cells cost many more cells.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2387Boundary sensorA sensor that reports whether the robot touches, or is close to, an obstacle, such as a bumper or a proximity sensor; it gives yes/no readings.Note RO-010Concept
G-2289Caster wheelA free-swivelling, undriven wheel, like the one under an office chair; it supports a robot without steering it.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2315Complete stateA state that, once known, makes earlier states, controls and measurements useless for predicting the future (position plus speed for a coasting robot, not position alone); it lets the robot keep only its latest estimate.Note RO-007State, controls and measurements
G-2524Consistent filterA filter whose real errors are as large as its own reported covariance says, on average; only then can its uncertainty be trusted by a controller or planner.Note RO-018Filter consistency
G-2298Control input uThe numbers we choose to drive a robot, such as u=(v,ω); the model turns them into motion.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2281Coordinate frameA chosen origin and set of axes used to give positions as numbers; every position or pose is stated relative to some frame.Note RO-001Pose
G-2448Correction step (measurement update)The Bayes-filter step after a reading: multiply each state’s predicted belief by the measurement probability p(zt​∣xt​) and rescale so the beliefs add to 1; it raises the states that explain the reading and sharpens the belief.Note RO-014Bayes filter
G-2396Correlative scan matchingScan matching that scores every candidate motion on a grid of shifts and turns and keeps the best, so it needs no good first guess.Note RO-011Concept
G-2311Dead reckoningWorking out a robot’s position from a known start by adding up its own moves, without looking at its surroundings; simple, but its error grows with every move, so it needs readings to correct it.Note RO-007Uncertainty in robotics
G-8δ (Huber)The error size at which Huber loss switches from squaring the error to taking its absolute value. It is a setting chosen before training (a hyperparameter).Note DL-014Huber loss
G-2386Depth-mapping sensorA sensor that reports the distance to the nearest surface along each of many directions, such as a laser scanner or a ring of sonars; the beam model describes its readings.Note RO-010Concept
G-2288Differential driveA robot with two independently driven wheels on one axle (plus a caster); it steers by running the wheels at different speeds and can spin on the spot.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2394Distance transformA grid that stores, for every cell of a map, the distance to the nearest occupied cell (with straight-line distances, the Euclidean distance transform); it lets a likelihood field be built in one pass.Note RO-011Concept
G-2296Dot notation x˙A dot over a quantity means its rate of change per second (its derivative with respect to time), such as x˙=0.433 m/s; models of motion are written with it.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2441Dynamic Bayes networkA Bayesian network that repeats the same variables at every time step, such as states, commands and readings of a robot; it shows which variable depends on which over time, so a whole run’s probability splits into small factors.Note RO-013Hidden Markov model
G-9ϵ (epsilon)A tiny number added to the variance to avoid dividing by 0; 0.001 in Keras.Note DL-031Batch normalisation
G-2299Euler stepOne step of predicting motion: hold the rates fixed for a short time Δt and add rate times Δt to each quantity; repeated, it traces a path, more accurately the smaller Δt is.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2402Expected range and bearing (r^,φ^​)The range and bearing a landmark would show from a guessed pose: the straight-line distance to its place in the map, and its direction (by atan2) minus the robot’s heading; the model compares the real reading with them.Note RO-012Concept
G-2375Expected range z∗The distance a beam would read with a perfect sensor, if the robot were at a given pose in the map; the measurement model compares each real reading with it.Note RO-010Concept
G-2520Extended Kalman filter (EKF)The Kalman filter for nonlinear motion and sensor models: it moves the mean through the nonlinear functions and uses their Jacobians at the latest estimate in place of F and H, so it can track unimodal beliefs through nonlinear models.Note RO-018Extended Kalman filter
G-2341Feature extraction (from sensor data)Pulling a few distinctive objects out of raw sensor data, such as two poles out of a 360-beam laser scan; it shrinks hundreds of numbers to a short list that is easy to match with a map.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2334Feature-based mapA map that stores only landmarks, each with its coordinates and signature, such as (1, 3, pink); very compact, but it says nothing about which space is free.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2469Filtering (state estimation)Estimating the current state from the readings so far, p(xt​∣z1:t​); what a robot needs while it drives, and what the Bayes filter computes.Note RO-015Hidden Markov model
G-2519First-order uncertainty propagationCarrying a mean and a standard deviation through a function by its value and slope at the mean: mean out ≈ h(μ), standard deviation out ≈ slope × standard deviation in (with a Jacobian, JPJT); accurate when the function is nearly straight across the standard deviation.Note RO-018Extended Kalman filter
G-2294Forward kinematics (wheeled robot)Working out the robot’s linear and angular velocity from its wheel speeds, used to predict where the robot goes.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2472Forward probability αt​The probability of the readings up to time t together with being in state x at t; the histogram filter before rescaling, carrying the evidence from the past.Note RO-015Hidden Markov model
G-2471Forward-backward algorithmThe method that computes smoothed beliefs in an HMM by multiplying a forward pass (evidence up to t) by a backward pass (evidence after t) and rescaling; it uses every reading of a recorded run for each time step.Note RO-015Hidden Markov model
G-10γ (gain) and β (shift)Two numbers per feature that layer normalisation learns in training: after the values are normalised, γ rescales them and β shifts them.Note DL-080Layer normalisation
G-11γ (scale) and β (shift)The two learnable parameters per node of a batch normalisation layer: after normalising, the layer multiplies by γ and adds β, so the network can choose its own mean and spread; they start at 1 and 0 in Keras.Note DL-031Batch normalisation
G-2336Half-planeAll points on one side of a line, together with the line: the points where ax+by+c≤0; one sign test, used as a building block for polygon obstacles.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-12μ^​An estimate of the population mean μ (the hat marks an estimate): a value computed from samples, here the mean of the sample means, used in place of the unknown μ.Note MA-034Central limit theorem
G-2284Heading θThe angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward.Note RO-001Pose
G-2439Hidden Markov model (HMM)A Markov chain whose states cannot be seen, where each state produces an observation that can, such as hidden robot cells producing “door” or “wall” readings; it is the model behind robot state estimation, speech recognition and many trackers.Note RO-013Hidden Markov model
G-2461Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter)The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z∣x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position.Note RO-015Histogram filter
G-2378Hit part phit​ (measurement noise in the beam model)The small scatter of a reading around the true distance when the beam does hit the mapped surface; modelled as a Gaussian around z∗ cut to [0,zmax​].Note RO-010Concept
G-2301Holonomic constraintAn equation on a robot’s pose, such as a train on a circular track x2+y2=25, or a velocity rule that follows from one; it removes whole poses the system can never be in.Note RO-001Nonholonomic constraints
G-2494Importance weightThe weight a particle gets from a reading: the height of the sensor model p(z∣x) at that reading, normalised over all particles; it says how well the particle explains what the robot sensed.Note RO-016Particle filter
G-2431Information state (history)Everything a robot knows at time t: its starting knowledge plus every command and every reading so far, such as (stay, door, move 2, door); every decision must be based on it, because the true state is never seen.Note RO-013Belief
G-2511InnovationThe gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z−Hxˉ; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2523Innovation covariance SThe variance the filter expects of its next innovation, S=HPˉHT+R: prediction uncertainty seen through the sensor plus sensor noise; it scales the gain and is the yardstick for the NIS test.Note RO-018Filter consistency
G-13∫ab​f(x)dxThe area under f from a to b; for a PDF, P(a≤X≤b).Note MA-022Probability density function (PDF)
G-2529Instantaneous centre of curvature (ICC)The point a turning robot’s whole body circles at a given moment; for a differential drive it lies on the axle line at distance R=v/ω from the midpoint, so it fixes how fast each wheel must move.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2384Intrinsic parameters (of a sensor model)The numbers that describe a sensor and its surroundings rather than the pose, such as the beam model’s four weights, σhit​ and λshort​; they are learned from recorded readings.Note RO-010Concept
G-2295Inverse kinematics (wheeled robot)Working out the wheel speeds that give a wanted linear and angular velocity, used by a controller to command the motors.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2506Kalman filterThe Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2508Kalman gain KThe weight the update gives to the reading, K=pˉ​/(pˉ​+R) in one dimension: the weight that makes the updated variance smallest, near 1 when the prediction is vague and near 0 when the reading is.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2297Kinematic modelEquations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as x˙=vcosθ, y˙​=vsinθ, θ˙=ω; used to predict motion at low speed.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2405Known correspondenceKnowing which landmark of the map a reading belongs to, for example from a unique colour (its signature); with it the model can predict that one landmark’s range and bearing.Note RO-012Concept
G-2342LandmarkAn object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2401Landmark measurement modelThe density of a landmark reading (range, bearing) given a pose and the map: a Gaussian of the range error times a Gaussian of the bearing error, with the errors taken as independent; it scores how well a guessed pose explains what the robot saw.Note RO-012Concept
G-2385Landmark sensorA sensor that reports the direction or distance to a known point in the world, such as a camera that sees a coloured pole; each kind of report needs its own measurement model.Note RO-010Concept
G-2393Likelihood fieldA grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam.Note RO-011Concept
G-2391Likelihood field modelA measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part prand​, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam.Note RO-011Concept
G-2507Linear Gaussian systemA system whose next state and whose readings are linear functions of the state plus normal noise, starting from a normal belief; in it the belief stays normal, so the Kalman filter is exact.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2527Linear functionA function y=ax+b: a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, whose graph is a straight line; passing a normal variable through it gives another normal variable, which is why the Kalman filter is exact for linear models.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2291Linear velocity vHow fast a robot’s reference point (for a differential drive, the middle of the axle) moves along its heading, in m/s; for a differential drive, the average of the two wheel speeds, so it sets how fast the robot advances.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2398Local mapA small grid map built from the robot’s current readings alone, such as the cells holding a scan’s endpoints; map matching compares it with the global map.Note RO-011Concept
G-2318LocalizationWorking out a robot’s pose in a known map from the controls it sent and the measurements it received; needed because the pose itself cannot be measured directly.Note RO-007Uncertainty in robotics
G-2335Location-based map (grid map)A map that splits space into cells and stores a value for every cell, occupied or free, free space included (2800 cells for a 7 m by 4 m room at 0.1 m); larger, but it answers at once whether a pose is free.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2499Low-variance sampler (systematic resampling)A way to resample with one random start between 0 and 1/M and M pointers 1/M apart along the stacked weights; it keeps every particle with weight at least 1/M, adds little randomness and runs in time proportional to M.Note RO-016Particle filter
G-2331MapA robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2397Map matching (correlation-based)Scoring a guessed pose by placing a local map built from the scan on the global map there and computing their correlation, cut at zero; it is cheap but coarse, limited by the cell size.Note RO-011Concept
G-2329Map-consistent motion modelA motion model that also uses the map, approximated for small steps by multiplying the plain motion model by 1 for free poses and 0 for poses inside obstacles; it stops the robot’s estimate from passing through walls.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-2437Markov chainA sequence of random states in which the next state depends only on the current one, not on earlier ones, such as a robot repeating “move 2”; it lets a whole sequence be described by one table of transition probabilities.Note RO-013Hidden Markov model
G-2316Markov propertyThe property of a sequence of states that the future depends on the past only through the present state; it lets a filter forget the history and work from the latest state alone.Note RO-007State, controls and measurements
G-2373Maximum range zmax​The longest distance a range sensor can report, such as 5 m; when no pulse returns, the sensor reports this value, so a reading of zmax​ usually means a failure, not a wall.Note RO-010Concept
G-2380Max-range reading (pmax​)A reading of exactly zmax​ that a sensor gives when its pulse never returns (glass, black or shiny surfaces, nothing in range); modelled as a spike at zmax​.Note RO-010Concept
G-2521Measurement Jacobian HThe slopes of the sensor model at the predicted state, one row per reading and one column per state variable; the EKF uses it to compute the innovation covariance and the gain, and its size says how much a reading tells about the state.Note RO-018Extended Kalman filter
G-2515Measurement matrix HThe matrix that turns the state into the reading the sensor should give, such as H=[1,0] for a sensor that sees position but not speed.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2374Measurement model p(z∣x,m)The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose x in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings.Note RO-010Concept
G-2510Measurement noise RThe random error of a sensor reading, given as its variance or covariance R; it sets how much the filter trusts each reading and is taken from the datasheet or measured in a calibration.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2435Measurement probabilityThe probability of a sensor reading given the true state, p(zt​∣xt​), such as 0.6 for reading “door” in front of a door; it tells the robot how well each state explains a reading.Note RO-013Belief
G-2317Measurement zt​What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution.Note RO-007State, controls and measurements
G-2493Monte Carlo estimateAn estimate of a probability or an average made by counting or averaging random samples, such as the share of samples at door 3; it needs no formula for the distribution, and its standard deviation shrinks like one over the square root of the number of samples.Note RO-016Particle filter
G-2476Most likely pathThe one sequence of hidden states with the highest probability given all readings, such as cells 1, 3, 5; one consistent answer for a whole run, found by the Viterbi algorithm.Note RO-015Hidden Markov model
G-2522Motion Jacobian GThe table of slopes of the motion model at the last estimate, one row per new state variable and one column per old one; the EKF uses it to carry the covariance forward as GPGT+Q.Note RO-018Extended Kalman filter
G-2462Motion kernelThe short list of move probabilities, such as (0.1, 0.8, 0.1) for one cell short, exact, one cell too far, slid along the belief in the prediction step; it spreads each cell’s belief over the cells the robot may have reached.Note RO-015Histogram filter
G-2319Motion model p(xt​∣ut​,xt−1​)The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-2500Multinomial resamplingPlain resampling: M independent random numbers each pick a particle in proportion to weight; simple, but a good particle can get no copy by chance.Note RO-016Particle filter
G-2525NEES (normalised estimation error squared)The squared estimation error divided by the filter’s variance, x~TP−1x~; for a consistent filter it follows chi-square with n degrees of freedom and averages n, so its average over simulated runs tests consistency when the truth is known.Note RO-018Filter consistency
G-2526NIS (normalised innovation squared)The squared innovation divided by its predicted covariance, yTS−1y; for a consistent filter it follows chi-square with m degrees of freedom (one per reading) and averages m, so it tests consistency from readings alone, even on the robot.Note RO-018Filter consistency
G-2432Nondeterministic (set-valued) information stateThe set of states that agree with every command and reading so far, such as cells {1, 3, 7} after reading “door”; a move replaces it by all reachable states, a reading keeps only the states that fit, but it says nothing about how likely each state is.Note RO-013Belief
G-2302Nonholonomic constraintA rule on velocities that does not follow from any equation on the pose, such as a wheel that cannot slide sideways; it limits which way a robot can move at each moment but not which poses it can reach.Note RO-001Nonholonomic constraints
G-2530Nonlinear functionA function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x)=(6−x)2+4​; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it.Note RO-018Extended Kalman filter
G-2382Normalizer ηThe factor that rescales a set of numbers, or a density, so that they add up (or integrate) to 1; it is always one over the current total: the sum of the products in the Bayes filter (1/0.4 = 2.5 after a reading in the door world), the area under the cut curve in the beam model (1/0.655 = 1.53).Note RO-010Concept
G-2517ObservabilityWhether a system’s whole state can be worked out from its readings and commands over time; a filter needs it before it can pin down every state variable.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2340Occupancy gridA grid map that stores in each cell a number between 0 and 1, such as the probability that the cell is occupied, instead of a hard 0 or 1; the standard grid map of robotics, since sensors are never sure.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2322Odometry calibrationMeasuring one robot’s real wheel radii and wheel separation, for example by driving known paths, so that odometry has no systematic error; a 1 percent radius error alone puts a robot 2.49 m off after 10 m.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-2323Odometry motion modelA motion model that splits the pose change reported by odometry into a first turn, a straight drive and a second turn, and adds independent noise to each, with a standard deviation that grows with the motion; used when wheel encoders exist.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-2388Odometry sensorA sensor that reports how far the robot has moved, from counting wheel turns; robots usually feed it into the motion model rather than the measurement model.Note RO-010Concept
G-14∂L/∂b1​How much the loss changes when the convolution layer’s bias b1​ is nudged (the gradient of the loss with respect to b1​), used to update that bias. Because the one bias is added to every cell of the feature map, it is the sum of the feature map’s gradient over all its cells.Note DL-048Backpropagation in a CNN
G-15∂L/∂W1​How much the loss changes when each filter weight in W1​ is nudged (the gradient of the loss with respect to W1​), used to update the filter. It is found by sliding the feature map’s gradient over the input like a filter, a convolution of the input with that gradient.Note DL-048Backpropagation in a CNN
G-16∂L/∂zHow much the loss changes when a node’s weighted sum z changes (the derivative of the loss with respect to z). Every weight entering the node multiplies it by its own input.Note DL-016Backpropagation
G-17∂L/∂Z2​=a2​−yHow much the loss changes with the output’s weighted sum Z2​ (its gradient): for a sigmoid output with log loss it simplifies to prediction minus target, the error. It then gives the slope of every output weight and bias.Note DL-047Backpropagation in a CNN
G-2491ParticleOne sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief.Note RO-016Particle filter
G-2501Particle deprivationThe failure in which no particles are left near the true state, so the filter settles confidently on a wrong answer; caused by too few particles or unlucky resampling, and fought with more particles and fewer resamplings.Note RO-016Particle filter
G-2492Particle filterA Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors.Note RO-016Particle filter
G-18Φ(z)The probability that a standard normal value is below z: the area under the bell curve to the left of z (the CDF of the standard normal distribution). For example Φ(1)=0.84.Note MA-025Standard normal and the z-table
G-19ϕ(z)The height of the standard normal bell curve (mean 0, standard deviation 1) at z, which shows how densely values lie near z (its probability density function).Note MA-025Standard normal and the z-table
G-2383Point massA distribution that puts all its probability on one value, such as a reading of exactly zmax​; it has no density height, so code draws it as a very narrow box of area 1.Note RO-010Concept
G-2280PoseWhere a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x,y) and heading θ, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading.Note RO-001Pose
G-2436Predicted beliefThe belief after the latest command but before the latest reading, bel(xt​)=p(xt​∣z1:t−1​,u1:t​); it separates the doubt a move adds from the knowledge a reading brings.Note RO-013Belief
G-2512Predicted estimate (a priori)The estimate and its variance after the predict step and before the step’s reading, xˉ and pˉ​; it says what the model alone expects.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2447Prediction step (motion update)The Bayes-filter step after a command: for each state, add up the probability of reaching it from every previous state, weighted by the belief in that state, bel(xt​)=∑p(xt​∣ut​,xt−1​) bel(xt−1​); it moves the belief with the robot and usually widens it, because the motion is uncertain; a near-certain command, such as a push that opens a door, can make the belief sharper.Note RO-014Bayes filter
G-2451Probabilistic information stateThe belief viewed as a summary of the robot’s history: a probability distribution over states that can be updated from itself, the newest command and the newest reading, so it carries everything the history knew and the history can be discarded.Note RO-014Bayes filter
G-2313Probabilistic roboticsThe approach in which a robot keeps a probability distribution over what might be the case (such as where it is) instead of one best guess, so it can handle ambiguous readings and recover from errors.Note RO-007Uncertainty in robotics
G-2509Process noise QThe random part of the motion the model leaves out (wheel slip, pushes), given as its variance or covariance Q; it widens the belief at every predict step and is usually set by tuning.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2285RadianThe unit of angle at which the arc of a circle is as long as its radius; a full turn is 2π rad, and with radians an arc is simply radius times angle.Note RO-001Pose
G-2381Random measurement (prand​)A reading with no modelled cause, such as cross-talk or a stray reflection; modelled as a uniform density 1/zmax​ (the uniform part prand​) so that no reading ever has density 0.Note RO-010Concept
G-2371Range finderA sensor that measures the distance to the nearest surface in one direction, for example by timing a laser or sound pulse; robots use it to compare what they see with a map.Note RO-010Concept
G-2343Range (of a landmark reading)The distance from the robot to a sensed landmark, such as 2.236 m; together with the bearing it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2372Range scanThe list of readings from one sweep of a scanning range finder, one distance per beam direction, such as z=(1.00,1.97,2.04,1.99); it is the measurement a laser-based robot tests poses against.Note RO-010Concept
G-2376Ray castingFinding the expected range by walking along a beam’s direction through the map until the first occupied cell; it turns a guessed pose and a map into the readings the robot should see.Note RO-010Concept
G-2450Recursive state estimationEstimating the state by updating the previous estimate with only the newest command and reading, instead of recomputing from the whole history; it keeps the work per step fixed however long the robot runs.Note RO-014Bayes filter
G-2330Rejection samplingDrawing samples and keeping only those that pass a test, drawing again otherwise; used to keep motion samples out of obstacles.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-2498Resampling (particle filter)Drawing a fresh set of M particles, with replacement, from the weighted set, each pick in proportion to weight, then giving all weight 1/M; heavy particles are copied and light ones dropped, so computation goes where the belief is.Note RO-016Particle filter
G-2290Rolling without slippingA wheel moving so that its contact point does not skid: it moves forward by its radius times the angle it turns and never slides sideways, which is what lets wheel turns predict motion.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2326Sampling (from a distribution)Drawing random values so that, over many draws, each value comes up as often as a given distribution says; it turns a motion model into a cloud of possible poses for particle filters.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-2408Sampling poses from a measurementDrawing poses that fit one reading: for a landmark, a random angle around it, the measured range plus noise, and the heading that makes the landmark appear at the measured bearing; used to add good guesses to a particle filter that is lost.Note RO-012Concept
G-2395Scan matchingAligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry.Note RO-011Concept
G-2312Sensor noiseSmall random errors in a sensor’s readings, so the same quantity measured twice gives slightly different numbers (a wall 2 m away reads 1.92 to 2.07 m); it is one reason a robot cannot take a reading at face value.Note RO-007Uncertainty in robotics
G-2345Signature (of a landmark)A label that says what kind of landmark was sensed, such as its colour or ID number; it tells the robot which landmark in the map a reading belongs to.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2470SmoothingEstimating the state at an earlier time using all readings, including later ones, p(xt​∣z1:T​); later readings often settle where the robot was, such as raising the true starting cell from 0.19 to 0.36.Note RO-015Hidden Markov model
G-2516State observerA model run alongside the real system and corrected by a gain times the gap between the measured and the predicted reading, so it rebuilds states no sensor measures for a controller to use; the Kalman filter is the observer with the best gain for the given noises.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2514State transition matrix FThe matrix that carries the state one step forward in a linear model, such as F=[[1,1],[0,1]] for position and speed with 1 s steps (position plus speed, speed unchanged).Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2434State transition probabilityThe probability of the next state given the command and the previous state, p(xt​∣ut​,xt−1​), such as 0.8 for “move 2” taking the robot from cell 1 to cell 3; it tells the robot how a command changes where it is.Note RO-013Belief
G-2314State xt​The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate.Note RO-007State, controls and measurements
G-2464Static decompositionCutting the state space into cells fixed before the robot starts, usually a regular grid such as 15 cm cells and 2° headings; simple, but it spends as much work on empty regions as where the robot is.Note RO-015Histogram filter
G-2467Static stateA state that the robot’s commands do not change while it is being estimated, such as a door nobody touches; the prediction step then does nothing and only readings update the belief.Note RO-015Binary Bayes filter
G-2518Steady-state gainThe fixed value the Kalman gain settles to once the variance added by each prediction balances the variance removed by each update, such as 0.22 for Q=0.01 and R=0.16.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-20Lognormal(μ,σ2)A short way to write a log-normal distribution: positive values with a long tail to the right (right-skewed), whose logarithm is normal, lnX∼N(μ,σ2).Note MA-029Log-normal distribution
G-21θ (theta)One symbol for all the parameters of a model.Note MA-070Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)
G-22ATAThe matrix A transposed times A, used to find the SVD by hand: it is symmetric, its eigenvectors are the right singular vectors of A and its eigenvalues are the squared singular values.Note MA-058Singular value decomposition
G-23bij​The number added to the weighted sum of node j in layer i before the activation (its bias), which lets the node shift its output.Note DL-008MLP notation and parameter count
G-24dk​The length of each key vector (and query vector); attention divides its scores by dk​​ so that long vectors do not give scores so spread out that the softmax puts almost all the weight on one word.Note DL-075Scaled dot-product attention
G-25dk​, dv​The size of each head’s query and key vectors (dk​) and value vectors (dv​); dmodel​/h=64 in the transformer.Note DL-078Multi-head attention
G-26dff​The width of the hidden layer of the transformer’s feed-forward network: each word’s 512-number vector is widened to dff​=2048 numbers, passed through ReLU, then brought back to 512.Note DL-081Transformer encoder
G-27dmodel​The number of values in each word’s vector at the layer’s input and output; 512 in the transformer.Note DL-078Multi-head attention
G-28hThe number of attention heads in multi-head attention: self-attentions run in parallel, each with its own view of the sentence; h=8 in the transformer, each head of size dmodel​/h=64.Note DL-078Multi-head attention
G-29ht(l)​In a deep RNN, layer l‘s summary of the sequence up to time step t (its hidden state); it feeds both the next time step and the layer above.Note DL-065Deep (stacked) RNNs
G-30Henc​The output of the last encoder block: one vector per input word, read by every decoder block.Note DL-084Transformer decoder
G-32N(μ,σ2)Notation for a normal distribution, the symmetric bell curve, with mean μ (its centre) and variance σ2 (its spread squared); X∼N(68,32) reads: X is normal with mean 68 and standard deviation 3.Note MA-024Normal distribution
G-33Oij​The one number that node j in layer i produces (its output), passed as input to every node of the next layer.Note DL-008MLP notation and parameter count
G-34P(X=x)The probability that the random variable X takes the value x.Note MA-021Probability mass function (PMF)
G-35P(X=x,Y=y)The joint probability that X takes the value x and Y the value y together.Note MA-014Joint and marginal probability
G-2475TrellisA grid drawing of an HMM run with one column of states per time step and lines for the possible moves between columns; every path through it is one guess at the hidden states.Note RO-015Hidden Markov model
G-2338Triangle meshA set of triangles, each given by three corner points in space, that together cover an object’s surface (a table as 12 triangles on 8 corners); fast to draw in 3D, but it does not say what is inside.Note RO-009Maps and landmarks
G-2406TrilaterationFinding a position from measured distances to points at known places: each distance puts the robot on a circle, and the circles meet at the position; GPS works this way.Note RO-012Concept
G-2293Turning radius RThe distance from the point a robot is turning about (the instantaneous centre of curvature, ICC) to the robot’s reference point; R=v/ω, so it says how tight a turn is.Note RO-001Differential-drive kinematics
G-2379Unexpected object (pshort​)Something not in the map, such as a person, that blocks the beam before the mapped surface and gives a short reading; modelled as an exponential from 0 up to z∗, because only the first blocker counts.Note RO-010Concept
G-2528UnimodalHaving a single mode (one peak); a unimodal belief can be held by one Gaussian, so the Kalman filter needs only its mean and variance.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-2513Updated estimate (a posteriori)The estimate and its variance after the reading has been blended in, x^ and p; it is the filter’s output for the step and the start of the next.Note RO-017Kalman filter
G-36V0​The value a running average (the EWMA) starts from: 0, or the first value θ1​.Note DL-033Exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA)
G-2324Velocity motion modelA motion model that takes the commanded linear velocity v and angular velocity ω, moves the robot along the exact arc about the ICC that they give, and adds noise to both speeds plus an extra final turn; used without encoders or to predict before a move.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-2474Viterbi algorithmThe method that finds the single most likely sequence of hidden states in an HMM by keeping, for each state and time, only the best path ending there and where it came from, then tracing back; it costs states squared times steps instead of trying every path.Note RO-015Hidden Markov model
G-38w0​The fixed number in the equation of a line, plane or hyperplane (the constant term). It shifts the hyperplane away from the origin, and is 0 when the hyperplane passes through the origin.Note MA-051Equation of a hyperplane
G-2320Wheel encoderA sensor that counts how far a wheel turns, for example a slotted disc on the shaft that gives one tick per slot passing a light sensor; its counts are the raw data of wheel odometry.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-2321Wheel odometryWorking out a robot’s pose by adding up the wheel motion its encoders measure: ticks to wheel distances, to the robot’s move and turn, to a new pose; accurate over short distances but it drifts, because every error stays in the sum.Note RO-008Probabilistic motion models
G-39Wi​, Wh​, Wo​The three weight matrices of an RNN: Wi​ multiplies the current input, Wh​ multiplies the hidden state fed back from the previous time step, and Wo​ turns the hidden state into the output.Note DL-056Recurrent neural network (RNN)
G-40WO​The learned output matrix that mixes the concatenated head outputs back to dmodel​ numbers per word.Note DL-078Multi-head attention
G-2282World frameThe coordinate frame fixed to the surroundings (for example a corner of the room), in which the robot’s pose is given.Note RO-001Pose
G-41WQ​, WK​, WV​The learned matrices that turn an embedding into its query, key and value vectors; the same for every word.Note DL-074Self-attention (query, key, value)
G-42Wup​, Wdown​The two learned matrices of the MLP block: Wup​ first widens each vector, Wdown​ then narrows it back. In GPT-2 they are named c_fc and c_proj.Note DL-089MLP blocks as fact storage
G-37Wijk​The weight entering layer k, from node i of layer k−1 to node j of layer k.Note DL-008MLP notation and parameter count
G-43xm​ (Pareto)The minimum possible value, where the Pareto curve starts and peaks.Note MA-030Pareto distribution and power laws
G-44Xdec​The decoder’s numbers for the output sentence (its representation), one row per output position, which go into cross-attention.Note DL-083Cross-attention
G-45Y∼Po(λ)Notation: Y follows a Poisson distribution with rate λ; likewise Bern(p) and B(n,p).Note MA-032Poisson distribution
G-46.dt accessorThe pandas tool that applies date and time methods to every value of a datetime column.Note ML-033Date and time features
G-47.str accessorThe pandas tool that applies a text method to every value of a column.Note ML-032Mixed variables
G-480-1 lossA loss that counts 1 for every misclassified point and 0 for every correct one.Note DL-006Perceptron loss
G-223610% conditionWhen sampling without replacement, keep the sample at most 10% of the population so the observations are roughly independent.Note MA-042T-tests: one-sample, two-sample, paired
G-492D density plotA plot that shows which pairs of values of two numerical features are common and which are rare (their joint density), usually as filled contours seen from above.Note MA-027Probability density function (PDF)
G-503D scatter plotA scatter plot with three numerical features on three axes, one point per observation, to see how the three relate at once.Note MA-007Frequency tables
G-514-3-2-1 networkA neural network named by its layer sizes, input first: 4 inputs, hidden layers of 3 and 2 nodes, and 1 output; the name gives the architecture in one line.Note DL-008MLP notation and parameter count
G-525% rule of thumbDrop the incomplete rows (complete case analysis) only for columns missing less than about 5% of their values, so only a small part of the data is lost.Note ML-034Complete case analysis
G-5368-95-99.7 rule (empirical rule)In a column shaped like a bell curve (a normal distribution), about 68.3%, 95.4% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.Note ML-041Z-score outlier method
G-5480-20 rule (Pareto principle)About 20% of the causes produce about 80% of the results, e.g. 20% of people hold 80% of the wealth.Note MA-030Pareto distribution and power laws
G-55@ (matrix multiplication)Python’s operator for multiplying matrices and vectors.Note ML-054Multiple linear regression
G-56<start> and <end> tokensSpecial tokens that tell the decoder to begin writing and mark the end of the output.Note DL-068Sequence-to-sequence (encoder-decoder)
G-57[CLS], [SEP]The special tokens BERT adds at the start and the end of every sentence.Note DL-078Multi-head attention
G-58add_indicator=TrueThe SimpleImputer setting that fills the gaps and also adds columns marking which values were missing (missing indicators), in one step.Note ML-037Simple imputation (mean, median, mode, constant)
G-59AddA layer that adds tensors of the same shape element by element.Note DL-054Skip connections
G-60alternative (scipy)The argument of scipy’s tests that sets which direction of difference the test looks for (the direction of H1​): "two-sided", "less" or "greater".Note MA-042T-tests: one-sample, two-sample, paired
G-61base_scoreXGBoost’s starting prediction, which every tree then corrects; for classification it is given as a probability, which XGBoost turns into log-odds.Note ML-119XGBoost
G-62batch_size=1Keras setting that updates the weights after every single row.Note DL-016Batch size in Keras
G-63batch_sizeKeras setting: the number of rows used for each update; n, 1 or in between gives batch, stochastic or mini-batch.Note DL-020Batch size in Keras
G-64BatchNormalizationThe Keras layer that applies batch normalisation: placed after a hidden layer, it standardises that layer’s values over each mini-batch and learns γ and β, which makes training faster.Note DL-031Batch normalisation
G-65BayesianRidgeA linear regression that keeps its weights small (built-in shrinkage); the default model of IterativeImputer.Note ML-039Iterative imputation (MICE)
G-66best_params_The best combination of settings found by GridSearchCV.Note ML-037Grid and random search
G-67BidirectionalThe Keras wrapper that makes any recurrent layer read the sequence both forwards and backwards (bidirectional).Note DL-066Bidirectional RNNs
G-68build_model(hp)The function that builds and compiles one network, asking hp for each tuned value.Note DL-039Keras Tuner
G-69bw_adjustseaborn’s multiplier on the KDE bandwidth it picks itself (not the bandwidth): values above 1 give a smoother curve, values below 1 a bumpier one.Note MA-023Kernel density estimation (KDE)
G-70clippandas method that moves every value below a lower bound up to it and every value above an upper bound down to it.Note ML-043Capping (winsorization)
G-71ConcatenateA layer that joins vectors end to end into one longer vector.Note DL-054Keras functional API
G-72Conv2DThe Keras layer that performs 2D convolution, Conv2D(filters, kernel_size): it slides learned filters over an image and outputs one feature map per filter.Note DL-042Convolution operation and feature maps
G-73cv_results_The scores of every combination tried by GridSearchCV.Note ML-037Grid and random search
G-74decode_predictionsThe function that turns 1,000 ImageNet probabilities into class names.Note DL-051Pretrained models and ImageNet
G-75Dropout layerKeras layer that switches off a fraction p of the previous layer’s outputs at each training step; inactive at prediction.Note DL-025Dropout
G-76EarlyStoppingThe Keras callback that stops training when a monitored quantity stops improving.Note DL-022Early stopping
G-77Embedding layerThe Keras layer that holds a table with one learned vector per word (the embedding matrix E) and looks up one row per word.Note DL-057Word embeddings
G-78enable_iterative_imputerThe import that switches on the experimental IterativeImputer.Note ML-039Iterative imputation (MICE)
G-79ewmThe pandas method for averages that weight recent values more (exponentially weighted calculations); its alpha =1−β.Note DL-033Exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA)
G-80fill_modeHow empty pixels after a shift or rotation are filled: nearest, reflect, constant or wrap.Note DL-050Data augmentation
G-81fill_valueThe value SimpleImputer uses with strategy="constant".Note ML-035Simple imputation (mean, median, mode, constant)
G-82fillnaThe pandas method that replaces every NaN with a given value.Note ML-035Simple imputation (mean, median, mode, constant)
G-83find, find_allReturn the first matching tag, or a list of all matching tags.Note ML-017Web scraping
G-84fitTrains the model on given inputs and outputs for a number of epochs.Note ML-012Supervised learning
G-85get_weights() / set_weights()Keras methods that read and replace the weight and bias arrays of a model or a layer, as a list of arrays.Note DL-029Weight initialisation
G-88GradientTapeTensorFlow’s tool that records a computation and returns its gradients automatically.Note DL-047Backpropagation in a CNN
G-89GridSearchCVThe scikit-learn class that tries every combination of settings in a grid, scores each by cross-validation, and keeps the best.Note ML-028Grid and random search
G-90hp.ChoiceTells the tuner that a setting to tune (a hyperparameter) takes one value from a list.Note DL-039Keras Tuner
G-91hp.FloatTells the tuner that a setting to tune (a hyperparameter) is a decimal number in a range; sampling="log" spreads its values evenly over powers of ten.Note DL-039Keras Tuner
G-92hp.IntTells the tuner that a setting to tune (a hyperparameter) is a whole number between a minimum and a maximum, with an optional step.Note DL-039Keras Tuner
G-93ignore_indexSetting of pd.concat that renumbers the joined rows from 0.Note ML-016APIs
G-94image_dataset_from_directoryThe Keras function that loads photos from class folders as batches of (images, labels).Note DL-049Image classification with a CNN (cats vs dogs)
G-95ImageDataGeneratorAn older Keras class for image augmentation: it makes randomly rotated, shifted, zoomed or flipped copies of training images; now deprecated in favour of image_dataset_from_directory and preprocessing layers.Note DL-050Data augmentation
G-96include_top=FalseThe keras.applications option that loads a pretrained model without its final dense layers (the dense top), which turn the found features into ImageNet’s 1,000 classes.Note DL-053Transfer learning (feature extraction and fine-tuning)
G-97Input (keras.Input)The Keras object that stands for a model’s input and fixes the shape of one input row.Note DL-054Keras functional API
G-98IterativeImputerscikit-learn’s class that fills missing values by predicting each feature with gaps from the other features, repeating until the fills settle (MICE). Still experimental, so it needs an extra import.Note ML-039Iterative imputation (MICE)
G-99json_normalizepandas function that turns nested JSON into flat columns.Note ML-016APIs
G-100keras.applicationsThe Keras module that provides famous pretrained networks with their weights.Note DL-051Pretrained models and ImageNet
G-101keras.datasets.mnistKeras’s built-in copy of MNIST, already split 60,000 / 10,000.Note DL-012ANN for classification
G-103keras.layers.AttentionKeras’ layer that lets each item of one sequence look at another sequence: it scores queries from the first against keys from the second by dot product (Luong-style attention). It returns the attention weights and the weighted sums of the values (context vectors).Note DL-077Attention mechanism
G-104keras.optimizers.SGDPlain gradient descent in Keras, with a fixed learning rate.Note DL-016Gradient descent
G-105kernel_initializerThe Dense argument that chooses how a layer’s weight matrix starts; default glorot_uniform.Note DL-030Weight initialisation
G-106kernel_regularizerKeras Dense setting that adds a penalty on the size of the layer’s weights (L1 or L2) to the loss.Note DL-026L1 and L2 regularisation in neural networks
G-107KernelDensityscikit-learn’s class that estimates a smooth density curve from data, using a chosen kernel and bandwidth (kernel density estimation). score_samples returns the log of the density, so apply np.exp.Note MA-023Kernel density estimation (KDE)
G-108KNNImputerscikit-learn’s class for KNN imputation: it fills each gap from the most similar observations (the nearest neighbours), using their values of that feature.Note ML-038KNN imputer
G-109lru_cachePython’s built-in tool that stores a function’s results automatically, so a repeated call reuses them (memoization).Note DL-019Memoization
G-110make_circlesscikit-learn function that generates two concentric rings of observations, one ring per class.Note DL-027Activation functions
G-111make_moonsscikit-learn function that generates two interleaving half-moon classes.Note DL-028Dying ReLU problem
G-112max_iter (IterativeImputer)The largest number of rounds IterativeImputer runs; default 10.Note ML-039Iterative imputation (MICE)
G-113max_iter (KMeans)The largest number of assign-and-move rounds k-means may run.Note ML-124K-means
G-114max_iter (LogisticRegression)The largest number of solver iterations; default 100, raised when a ConvergenceWarning appears.Note ML-080Logistic regression
G-115max_iter (SGDRegressor)The largest number of epochs (full passes over the training data) SGDRegressor runs before it stops, even if its stopping rule is not met; a ConvergenceWarning suggests raising it.Note ML-058Stochastic gradient descent
G-116MaxPooling2DThe Keras layer for 2D max pooling, MaxPooling2D(pool_size, strides): it keeps only the largest value in each window of a feature map, which shrinks the map; it has no parameters.Note DL-044Pooling
G-117min_child_weightXGBoost’s smallest allowed size of a leaf, measured as the sum of p(1−p) over its rows (in regression: the number of rows). A split that would leave a child below it is not made, which stops tiny leaves; default 1.Note ML-119XGBoost
G-118min_deltaThe smallest change of the monitored quantity that counts as an improvement.Note DL-022Early stopping
G-119MissingIndicatorThe scikit-learn class that builds columns marking which values were missing (missing indicators); features_ lists the columns with gaps.Note ML-037Missing indicator
G-120model.summary()Prints each layer’s output shape and number of trainable parameters.Note DL-011Keras workflow
G-121MultiHeadAttentionThe Keras layer that computes multi-head attention: it learns WQ​, WK​, WV​ and an output matrix and applies scaled dot-product attention; with num_heads=1 it is a single attention.Note DL-075Multi-head attention
G-122n_neighbors (k)The number of nearest rows the KNN imputer averages; default 5.Note ML-038KNN imputer
G-123normalize (pd.crosstab)Turns counts into probabilities: "all" joint, "index" per row, "columns" per column.Note MA-014Joint and marginal probability
G-124np.whereNumPy function that picks one value where a condition is true and another where it is false.Note ML-041Capping (winsorization)
G-125pd.concatpandas function that joins several DataFrames into one.Note ML-017Web scraping
G-126preprocess_inputThe function that prepares pixels the way a given pretrained model expects.Note DL-051Pretrained models and ImageNet
G-127quantilepandas method that returns a percentile, given as a fraction (0.25 for the 25th).Note ML-042IQR outlier method
G-128random_stateA seed that fixes a random draw, so the same code gives the same result.Note ML-037Random sample imputation
G-129RandomSearchA tuner that tries random combinations of the hyperparameter values.Note DL-039Keras Tuner
G-130read_jsonpandas function that reads JSON from a file or a URL into a DataFrame.Note ML-015JSON and SQL data
G-131read_sql_querypandas function that runs an SQL query and returns a DataFrame.Note ML-015JSON and SQL data
G-132reg_covarscikit-learn’s small number added to the diagonal of every covariance matrix in GaussianMixture, so no component shrinks into a spike on one point (collapses).Note MA-073Gaussian mixture model (GMM)
G-133RepeatVectorKeras layer that repeats one vector at several time steps.Note DL-058Types of RNN (many-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many)
G-134reset_afterKeras option: apply the reset gate after (default) or before the matrix product.Note DL-064GRU (gated recurrent unit)
G-135restore_best_weightsEarlyStopping setting that puts back the weights of the best epoch at the end.Note DL-022Early stopping
G-136return_sequencesArgument of a Keras recurrent layer: False returns only the last hidden state, True returns the hidden state at every time step; True is needed on every stacked layer but the last.Note DL-057Recurrent neural network (RNN)
G-138rhoKeras’ name for the number that sets how much of the past RMSProp’s running average keeps (its decay factor β); default 0.9.Note DL-037RMSProp
G-139same paddingJust enough padding to keep the output the size of the input (with stride 1).Note DL-043Padding and strides
G-140sample(n)The pandas method that draws n values at random from a Series or DataFrame.Note ML-037Random sample imputation
G-141sample_posteriorThe IterativeImputer setting that draws each fill at random from the model’s spread instead of using its single best prediction, so different seeds give several plausible filled tables.Note ML-039Iterative imputation (MICE)
G-143shuffle=FalseKeras setting that keeps the rows in their original order in every epoch.Note DL-016Backpropagation
G-144SimpleRNNThe Keras layer for a basic RNN; input shape (batch size, time steps, input features).Note DL-056Recurrent neural network (RNN)
G-145statistics_The fill values a fitted SimpleImputer has learned, one per column.Note ML-035Simple imputation (mean, median, mode, constant)
G-146step__param nameThe full name of a setting inside a pipeline: step names and the parameter joined by __.Note ML-028ML pipelines
G-147strategy="constant" (SimpleImputer)The SimpleImputer setting that fills every gap with fill_value.Note ML-036Simple imputation (mean, median, mode, constant)
G-148strategy="most_frequent" (SimpleImputer)The SimpleImputer setting for mode imputation: fit learns each column’s most frequent value and transform fills the gaps with it.Note ML-036Simple imputation (mean, median, mode, constant)
G-149strategy (KBinsDiscretizer)The KBinsDiscretizer parameter that chooses how the bin edges are set: uniform, quantile or kmeans binning.Note ML-031Binning and binarization
G-150strategy (SimpleImputer)The SimpleImputer parameter choosing the fill rule: mean, median, most_frequent or constant.Note ML-035Simple imputation (mean, median, mode, constant)
G-151to_categoricalKeras function that turns integer class labels into 0/1 vectors with a single 1 at the label’s position (one-hot encoding).Note DL-063Next-word prediction with an LSTM
G-152tolThe size of change below which IterativeImputer stops early; default 0.001.Note ML-039Iterative imputation (MICE)
G-153trainableThe Keras attribute that decides whether a layer’s weights are updated in training.Note DL-053Transfer learning (feature extraction and fine-tuning)
G-154use_causal_maskThe argument of Keras’ MultiHeadAttention that hides future tokens, so each token can attend only to itself and earlier tokens (the causal mask).Note DL-082Masked self-attention
G-155valid paddingNo padding; the output shrinks to n−f+1.Note DL-043Padding and strides
G-156validation_splitThe share of the training rows Keras holds back as a validation set.Note DL-011Keras workflow
G-157A/B testingComparing an old and a new version, of a model or a web page, by showing each to a random half of the users at the same time, to see which one does better.Note ML-009Beta and A/B testing
G-158Absolute positionA word’s place counted from the start of the sentence.Note DL-079Positional encoding
G-159Absolute valueA number’s size without its sign.Note ML-024Normalization
G-160absolute_errorA regression-tree setting (criterion) that chooses splits by the average size of the errors (mean absolute error); its leaves predict the median, so outliers pull less.Note ML-093Regression trees
G-161Accumulator vt​The running record of squared gradients that divides the learning rate.Note DL-037RMSProp
G-162AccuracyThe fraction of predictions that are correct.Note ML-012Accuracy
G-163Acquisition functionThe rule that picks the next trial using the stand-in model of the score (the surrogate), such as expected improvement.Note ML-128Bayesian optimisation
G-164Activation (ak)The vector of outputs of layer k; a0 is the input row.Note DL-010Forward propagation
G-165Activation functionThe function that turns a node’s weighted sum z into its output, bringing it into a fixed range.Note DL-004Activation functions
G-166Active constraintAn inequality constraint that the answer sits right on (it holds with equality), because the unconstrained minimum breaks it; it then acts like an equality constraint, and its multiplier can be positive.Note MA-066Lagrange multipliers, KKT and duality
G-167AdaBoost (Adaptive Boosting)A boosting algorithm that trains simple models (weak learners) one after another on reweighted data, and combines them by a vote in which each model counts by its alpha weight.Note ML-109AdaBoost
G-168AdaGradAn optimizer that gives each parameter its own learning rate, η/(vt​​+ϵ), where vt​ sums its past squared gradients.Note DL-036AdaGrad
G-169AdamAn optimizer, the rule that updates a network’s weights to reduce the loss: a variant of gradient descent that keeps running averages of past gradients and of their squares, giving each weight its own step size; fairly robust to its settings, so a common default.Note DL-038Adam
G-170AdamWAdam with weight decay (shrinking the weights a little) applied directly to the weights, not through the loss.Note DL-026L1 and L2 regularisation in neural networks
G-171Adaptive learning rateA learning rate that changes during training according to the gradients seen so far.Note DL-036AdaGrad
G-172Add and normAdds a sub-layer’s input back to its output (a residual connection) and then layer-normalises the sum, so the signal and gradients pass through deep stacks and the numbers stay on one scale: LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)).Note DL-081Residual connections and add & norm
G-173Addition rule (general addition rule)The rule for the probability that A or B (or both) happens: add their probabilities and subtract the overlap so it is not counted twice, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B); for mutually exclusive events the overlap is 0.Note MA-017Empirical vs theoretical probability, probability rules
G-174Additive modellingBuilding a complex function as a sum of simple functions, each capturing part of what the others missed.Note ML-115Gradient boosting
G-175Adjusted Rand index (ARI)A score for how well a clustering matches the true groups: 1 for identical, about 0 for random.Note MA-073Gaussian mixture model (GMM)
G-177Adjusted R²A version of R² with a penalty for each feature the model uses, so it rises only when a new feature truly helps; plain R² can creep up even when the new feature is useless.Note ML-051Regression metrics
G-178Affine transformationA linear transformation followed by a shift, Ax+b.Note MA-053Linear transformations and matrices
G-179AgentThe learner in reinforcement learning, such as a self-driving car or a game-playing program: it acts in an environment, gets rewards or punishments, and improves its rules for acting.Note ML-003Reinforcement learning
G-180Agglomerative clusteringGrouping that starts with one cluster per point and repeatedly merges the closest pair (bottom-up hierarchical clustering).Note ML-125Hierarchical clustering
G-181AgglomerativeClusteringscikit-learn’s class for agglomerative clustering: given the number of clusters, the distance and the linkage, fit_predict merges points bottom-up and returns each point’s cluster.Note ML-125Hierarchical clustering
G-182AggregateOne summary number (mean, median, maximum, …) computed from a group of values.Note MA-007Frequency tables
G-183Aggregation (in an ensemble)Combining the base models’ predictions into one: mode for classes, mean for numbers.Note ML-099Bagging
G-184AGI (artificial general intelligence)A machine with all the abilities of human intelligence. Does not exist yet.Note ML-002Artificial intelligence
G-185AI winterA period when funding and interest in AI collapse.Note DL-003History of deep learning
G-186AlertIn a pandas profiling report, a warning about a column that may need attention, such as many missing values; a question to check, not a verdict.Note ML-021Pandas Profiling
G-187AlexNetA deep convolutional neural network, trained on GPUs, that won the ImageNet contest in 2012 with about 15% error against about 26% for the next best entry, starting the current wave of deep learning.Note DL-051Pretrained models and ImageNet
G-2164Algorithm chooserA flowchart from a problem’s properties to suitable algorithms.Course map
G-191AlignmentWhich input words each output word relates to; read from the cross-attention weights.Note DL-069Attention mechanism
G-188Alignment gridA plot of how much each output word draws on each input word (all attention weights αij​ of a sentence pair), output words against input words.Note DL-069Attention mechanism
G-189Alignment modelThe small feed-forward network that scores how well encoder state hj​ fits the previous decoder state si−1​, giving the alignment score eij​.Note DL-069Attention mechanism
G-190Alignment score eij​How strongly encoder state j fits decoder step i, as a raw score before the softmax turns the scores into attention weights.Note DL-069Attention mechanism
G-192Alpha (model weight)A base model’s say in AdaBoost’s final vote; larger when it made fewer mistakes.Note ML-109AdaBoost
G-193Alternative hypothesis (H1​, Ha​)The claim of an effect, difference or relationship: the statement that contradicts the null hypothesis H0​.Note MA-038Hypothesis testing: null and alternative
G-2155AmbiguityHow much the ensemble’s members disagree: the spread of their predictions around their mean. It is the amount by which the vote’s squared error beats the average member’s.Note ML-098Voting ensembles
G-195AnacondaA free bundle (distribution) for data science that installs Python, hundreds of popular libraries and tools such as Jupyter in one go, with the conda package manager to keep them working together.Note ML-011Setup: conda, Jupyter and Colab
G-194Anaconda NavigatorAnaconda’s point-and-click window for environments and packages.Note ML-011Setup: conda, Jupyter and Colab
G-196Analogy question”a is to b as c is to ?”, answered by the word closest to c−a+b.Note DL-072Meaning as direction in embedding space
G-197Analytic functionA function that can be written exactly as its Taylor series (an infinite sum of powers) near every point.Note MA-061Taylor series
G-198AND gateA rule that outputs “yes” only when all its inputs are “yes”.Note DL-089MLP blocks as fact storage
G-199AND, ORLogic functions: 1 when both inputs are 1 (AND), or when at least one is (OR).Note DL-007Problem with the perceptron (XOR)
G-200Anderson-Darling testA statistical test of whether data follows a given distribution, such as the normal; like the Shapiro-Wilk test, it decides with a p-value.Note MA-028Kurtosis and moments
G-201Anomaly detectionFinding rows that do not fit the pattern of the rest.Note ML-003Anomaly detection
G-203ANOVAA test of whether several groups have the same mean (analysis of variance).Note MA-046One-way ANOVA
G-202ANOVA tableThe standard table that sets out an ANOVA’s results: for each source of variation (between groups, within groups) it lists the sum of squares, degrees of freedom, mean square, the F statistic and the p-value.Note MA-046One-way ANOVA
G-204API (Application Programming Interface)A service that returns data when our code asks for it; a website’s API hands out its data on request.Note ML-007APIs
G-205API keyA secret code that tells the API who is asking.Note ML-016APIs
G-206API tokenA secret file or key that lets a program use a website’s API as us.Note ML-011Setup: conda, Jupyter and Colab
G-207Approximate tree learning (histogram-based training)Finding a tree split by cutting each feature into bins and trying only the bin edges instead of every value; the split may be a little worse, but training is much faster.Note ML-117XGBoost
G-208Arbitrary value imputationFilling every gap with one fixed value that never occurs, such as 99 or −1.Note ML-035Simple imputation (mean, median, mode, constant)
G-209Architecture (of a network)How a network’s nodes are connected: how many, of what kind, and which connections.Note DL-002Neural networks
G-210arg maxThe value of the variable that makes an expression largest.Note ML-082Naive Bayes
G-211Arg min (argmin)The value of a variable that makes an expression smallest, written argmin.Note ML-115Gradient boosting
G-212argmaxThe position of the largest value; on 10 class probabilities, the predicted class.Note DL-012ANN for classification
G-214ArrayA grid of numbers with any number of dimensions (1D a list, 2D a list of lists); the programming name for a tensor. In NumPy every tensor is an array, an ndarray.Note ML-010Tensors
G-215Artificial Intelligence (AI)The field of building machines that show intelligence.Note ML-002Artificial intelligence
G-216Artificial neural network (ANN)The simplest neural network: neurons in layers, each layer connected to the next by weights.Note DL-002Neural networks
G-217ASICA chip custom-made for one job, such as the TPU.Note DL-002What deep learning is
G-218Association rule learningFinding items that tend to occur together.Note ML-003Association rule learning
G-219AssociativityA property of matrix multiplication: in a product of three matrices, which pair is multiplied first does not change the result, because both groupings mean apply C, then B, then A; written (AB)C=A(BC).Note MA-054Matrix multiplication as composition
G-220Assumption (of a model)A condition the data must meet for the model’s results to be reliable.Note ML-055Assumptions of linear regression
G-221AsymptoticComing ever closer to a line without touching it, like the normal curve’s tails and the x axis.Note MA-024Normal distribution
G-222Atomic valueA cell that holds one single piece of information, not several pushed into one place; tidy data needs it, because facts packed into one cell cannot be plotted, grouped or given to a model separately.Note ML-044Feature construction and splitting
G-226AttentionA mechanism that lets each output step weigh all input positions and focus on the useful ones.Note DL-069Attention mechanism
G-223Attention scoreA number that measures how strongly one word relates to another: the dot product of the first word’s query with the second word’s key. The softmax turns one word’s scores into its attention weights.Note DL-074Self-attention (query, key, value)
G-225Attention weightHow much one word draws on another word when building its new vector: an attention score after the softmax, so the weights of one word are non-negative and sum to 1.Note DL-074Self-attention (query, key, value)
G-224Attention weight αij​How much encoder state j counts at decoder step i; the weights of one step are non-negative and sum to 1.Note DL-069Attention mechanism
G-227Attentional hidden state h~i​In Luong attention, the vector the output layer reads to predict the next word: the decoder state and the context vector joined and passed through a tanh layer, h~i​=tanh(Wc​[ci​;si​]).Note DL-070Luong (multiplicative) attention
G-228AttributeAn extra setting written inside an HTML opening tag as name="value", such as a class; scrapers use attributes to pick out the right tags.Note ML-017Web scraping
G-229AUCA single score for a classifier from 0.5 (random) to 1 (perfect): the area under its ROC curve.Note ML-077ROC curve and AUC
G-230AutocorrelationWhen each residual is related to the one before it in row order (too high on one observation, too high on the next), as is common in time series; linear regression assumes there is none.Note ML-055Assumptions of linear regression
G-231AutoencoderA network with a narrow middle layer that learns to compress data and rebuild it.Note DL-003Types of neural networks
G-232Automatic differentiationSoftware that computes exact derivatives of a program by the chain rule on its elementary operations; reverse mode is backpropagation.Note MA-063Jacobian and matrix gradients
G-233Autoregressive (causal) generationProducing one output at a time, each chosen from the outputs already produced and fed back as input for the next.Note DL-082Masked self-attention
G-234Autoregressive modelA model that generates a sequence one item at a time, each item conditioned on the items it generated before.Note DL-082Masked self-attention
G-236Average linkageA way to measure the distance between two clusters in hierarchical clustering: the mean of all distances between a point of one cluster and a point of the other; the closest two clusters are merged next.Note ML-125Hierarchical clustering
G-237Average meaningWhat a static embedding stores: the word’s meaning averaged over all its uses in the training corpus.Note DL-073Contextual embeddings
G-238Average poolingPooling that replaces each window of a feature map with the mean of its values, which shrinks the map; unlike max pooling, it fades strong values such as edges.Note DL-044Pooling
G-239Average record sizeThe memory one row takes, on average.Note ML-021Pandas Profiling
G-240Axioms of probabilityThe three rules every probability obeys: non-negative, P(S)=1, mutually exclusive events add.Note MA-011Empirical vs theoretical probability, probability rules
G-242AxisOne direction along which a tensor’s numbers are arranged, used to say which way an operation runs; a matrix has two axes, down the rows (axis 0) and across the columns (axis 1).Note ML-010Tensors
G-241Axis of rotationThe line a 3D rotation leaves in place: an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1.Note MA-056Eigenvectors and eigenvalues
G-243Axis-parallel splitA cut that tests one column, so it is a line, plane or hyperplane parallel to the other axes.Note ML-091Decision trees
G-244B2BBusiness to business: a product that helps a company run its business.Note ML-008Applications of ML
G-245B2CBusiness to customer: a product sold to ordinary users.Note ML-008Applications of ML
G-247BackpropagationThe algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight and bias by applying the chain rule backward from the output; gradient descent then uses these gradients to train the network.Note DL-015Backpropagation
G-246Backpropagation through time (BPTT)Backpropagation for an RNN: the chain rule runs back over the network unfolded in time, adding up the gradient from every time step at which a shared weight is used.Note DL-059Backpropagation through time (BPTT)
G-248Backward eliminationFeature selection that starts with all columns and removes the worst at a time.Note ML-022Feature selection
G-249Backward passComputing the gradient of the loss for every tensor, from the output back to the input.Note DL-048Backpropagation in a CNN
G-250Bag of wordsThe simplest way to turn texts into feature vectors: list every unique word (the vocabulary), give each word one dimension, and count how often each word appears in the text.Note MA-048Bag of words
G-251Bagging (bootstrap aggregation)Training many models on different random samples of the data and averaging them, so the result depends less on the particular sample (lower variance).Note ML-095Bagging
G-252Bagging regressorA bagging ensemble of regressors that predicts the mean of their predictions.Note ML-101Bagging
G-253BaggingClassifierscikit-learn class for bagging, pasting, random subspaces and random patches in classification.Note ML-100Bagging
G-254BaggingRegressorscikit-learn class for bagging, pasting, random subspaces and random patches in regression.Note ML-101Bagging
G-255Bahdanau attention (additive)Attention whose alignment score comes from a small network with one hidden layer, fed the previous decoder state and one encoder state, v⊤tanh(Wa​si−1​+Ua​hj​); the score decides how much that encoder state counts. Called additive because the two terms are added inside the tanh.Note DL-070Bahdanau (additive) attention
G-256Balanced random forestA random forest for imbalanced data: every tree is trained on a balanced sample, the minority observations plus the same number of random majority observations, and the trees then vote.Note ML-127Balanced random forest
G-257BandwidthHow wide each kernel is in a KDE (for a Gaussian kernel, its standard deviation); it sets how smooth the estimated curve is.Note MA-023Kernel density estimation (KDE)
G-258Bar plotA plot for comparing a numerical column across categories: one bar per category, its height the mean of the numerical column for that category.Note ML-020Bivariate and multivariate analysis
G-259base environmentThe environment the installer creates, holding conda itself.Note ML-011Setup: conda, Jupyter and Colab
G-260Base modelOne of the models inside an ensemble; the ensemble combines the base models’ answers into its prediction.Note ML-095Ensemble learning
G-261Base prediction (F0​)The first model of gradient boosting; for regression, the mean of the target.Note ML-114Gradient boosting
G-2270BaselineA simple rule whose score a model must beat to show it has learned something.Note DL-063Next-word prediction with an LSTM
G-262BasisA set of vectors that are linearly independent and whose span is the whole space, so every vector can be built by scaling the basis vectors and adding them; a vector’s coordinates are those scales.Note MA-052Linear combinations, span and basis
G-263Batch (mini-batch)A small group of training observations used for one update; Keras uses 32 by default.Note ML-059Mini-batch gradient descent
G-264Batch gradient descentGradient descent that uses all training rows for every update.Note ML-057Batch gradient descent
