G-1700RobustnessPerforming well even when the data changes somewhat.Note ML-095Ensemble learning
G-1701RobustScalerscikit-learn’s class for robust scaling.Note ML-024Feature scaling
G-1702ROC curveA plot of the true positive rate against the false positive rate as the classification threshold moves; it shows a binary classifier’s trade-off at every threshold, and a curve nearer the top-left corner is better.Note ML-077ROC curve and AUC
G-1703RollbackRestoring a model to an earlier, good version.Note ML-005Online learning
G-1704Root mean squareThe square root of the average of squared values: the typical size of the gradients.Note DL-037RMSProp
G-1705Root mean squared error (RMSE)The square root of the average squared error (MSE), so the error is back in the output’s units.Note ML-051Regression metrics
G-1706Root nodeThe first node of a tree, holding all the training rows.Note ML-091Decision trees
G-1709RotationA transformation that turns space without stretching or flipping it (an orthogonal matrix with determinant +1).Note MA-057Singular value decomposition
G-1708Rotation matrixThe matrix of a rotation about the origin; by 90°, columns [0,1] and [−1,0].Note DL-079Positional encoding
G-1707Rotation matrix Mk​The fixed matrix that turns the encoding of any position p into that of p+k.Note DL-079Positional encoding
G-1710Rotation, shift, zoom, shearFour common data-augmentation changes to an image: turning it, moving it, enlarging or shrinking it, and slanting it; each makes a new training image with the same label.Note DL-050Data augmentation
G-1711Row and column totalsThe sums in the margins of a contingency table; each counts one whole event.Note MA-013Venn diagrams and contingency tables
G-2245Row formWriting points as rows and multiplying xTWT; the matrix applied first is on the left.Note MA-054Matrix multiplication as composition
G-1712Row samplingGiving each base model a random subset of the rows.Note ML-102Random forest
G-1713Row spaceAll the combinations of a matrix’s rows (their span), a subspace of the input space; the SVD’s right singular vectors vi​ with σi​>0 are a perpendicular basis of it.Note MA-058Singular value decomposition
G-1714Row vectorA vector written as one row, shape 1×n.Note MA-048Vectors and feature vectors
G-1715RPMRevolutions per minute: how fast a motor turns.Note ML-008Applications of ML
G-1716Runge’s phenomenonThe large swings of a high-degree polynomial near the ends of the interval it is fitted on.Note ML-115Gradient boosting
G-1717R² score (coefficient of determination)1 minus the model’s squared error divided by the squared error of always predicting the mean: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than the average.Note ML-051Regression metrics
G-1718Saddle pointA flat point that curves up in one direction and down in another.Note DL-032Local minima and saddle points
G-1719Safety (of an augmentation)Whether a transformation keeps the label true.Note DL-050Data augmentation
G-1720sagaA solver (the method that finds the weights) that updates them from randomly chosen rows (stochastic) and supports every penalty, including Elastic Net.Note ML-080Logistic regression
G-1721Same-length many-to-manyMany-to-many with one output per input time step.Note DL-058Types of RNN (many-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many)
G-1722SAMMEThe AdaBoost variant in scikit-learn: alpha without the factor 1/2, only misclassified rows reweighted; same decisions.Note ML-111AdaBoost
G-1723SAMME.RAn AdaBoost variant that used predicted probabilities; removed from scikit-learn.Note ML-112AdaBoost
G-1731SampleThe part of a population that we actually measure, such as 50,000 people asked about their salary instead of everyone in India; we study it because measuring the whole population is usually impossible, and use it to draw conclusions about the population.Note ML-007Population, sample, parameter and statistic
G-1724Sample covariance (sxy​)Covariance computed from a sample of n observations: the products of the two features’ distances from their means, added up and divided by n−1; its sign says whether the two features rise together or move in opposite directions.Note MA-009Covariance and covariance matrix
G-1725Sample mean (xˉ)The average of the values in a sample, xˉ: add them up and divide by n; it is used as the estimate of the population mean μ.Note MA-005Measures of central tendency
G-1726Sample proportion p^​The share of a sample that falls in one category, written p^​, such as 26 men out of 60; it estimates that share in the whole population.Note MA-044One-sample proportion test
G-1727Sample size (n)The number of values in one sample, written n, such as 50 people; a larger n makes the sample mean vary less from sample to sample (its spread is σ/n​).Note MA-033Sampling distribution and standard error
G-1728Sample skewness G1​The skewness formula used on a sample, G1​: the average cubed standardized distance from the mean, with a small-sample correction; it measures how lopsided the data is, and it is what pandas’ skew() returns.Note MA-026Skewness
G-1729Sample spaceThe set of all possible outcomes of an experiment, such as {1,…,6} for a die; every event is a subset of it, so probabilities are worked out inside it.Note MA-010Events and sample spaces
G-2229Sample variance s2The variance computed from a sample, s2: the squared distances from the sample mean, summed and divided by n−1; dividing by n−1 instead of n makes it right on average as an estimate of the population variance.Note MA-006Variance
G-1730Sample weightA number attached to each row saying how important it is; AdaBoost starts every row at 1/n and raises the weights of misclassified rows so the next model focuses on them.Note ML-110AdaBoost
G-1732sample_weightThe argument of fit that tells a scikit-learn model how much each row counts.Note ML-111AdaBoost
G-1733SamplerIn Optuna, the algorithm that suggests the next trial’s hyperparameter values.Note ML-128Optuna
G-1739Sampling (text generation)Choosing the next token at random according to the softmax probabilities, instead of always taking the most probable token, so the generated text does not keep repeating itself.Note DL-088Unembedding, logits, temperature and sampling
G-1734Sampling biasA sample that misrepresents the population because of how the data was collected, such as asking only Indian fans who should win a cricket match; a larger sample does not fix it.Note ML-007Sampling noise and bias
G-1736Sampling distributionThe distribution of a statistic (such as the mean) computed from many independent samples of the same size from one population; it shows how much that statistic varies from sample to sample.Note MA-033Sampling distribution and standard error
G-1735Sampling distribution of the sample meanThe distribution of the means of many samples of size n; by the central limit theorem it is close to normal, centred on the population mean, with spread σ/n​.Note MA-033Sampling distribution and standard error
G-1737Sampling noiseError in a sample’s result because the sample is too small, so the answer depends on luck, such as asking only 5 fans; a larger sample reduces it.Note ML-007Sampling noise and bias
G-1738Sampling techniquesWays of drawing a sample from a population so that it is random and representative, and its conclusions hold for the population.Note MA-004Population, sample, parameter and statistic
G-1740Saturated softmaxA softmax whose inputs are so far apart that one weight is near 1 and the rest near 0; its gradient is then near 0, so training barely changes the scores.Note DL-075Scaled dot-product attention
G-1741Saturating functionA function that squeezes any input into a bounded range, such as the sigmoid into 0 to 1, so its slope goes to 0 at the ends; those near-zero slopes make gradients vanish in deep networks.Note DL-027Activation functions
G-1743ScalarA single number, such as 5 or -6: a 0D tensor; multiplying a vector by it scales the vector, which is where the name comes from.Note ML-010Tensors
G-1742Scalar productAnother name for the dot product: multiply two vectors component by component and add, giving one number (a scalar) that is large when the vectors point the same way.Note MA-050Dot product
G-1744Scale (in SciPy)SciPy’s parameter for the exponential distribution, the average wait 1/λ.Note MA-071Exponential distribution
G-1745Scaled dot-product attentionSelf-attention in which every query–key dot-product score is divided by dk​​ before the softmax, so the scores do not spread so wide that the softmax saturates: softmax(QKT/dk​​)V.Note DL-075Scaled dot-product attention
G-1746Scaling (a vector)Multiplying or dividing every component of a vector by the same scalar, such as 2×[1,3]=[2,6]; it makes the arrow longer or shorter along the same line.Note MA-049Vector magnitude, distance and scalar operations
G-1747Scaling factorThe number 1/dk​​ that multiplies every attention score; it shrinks the spread of the scores so the softmax does not saturate.Note DL-075Scaled dot-product attention
G-1749Scatter plotA chart with one dot per row and one numerical column on each axis; it shows by eye whether two features rise together, fall together or are unrelated.Note ML-020Bivariate and multivariate analysis
G-1750scikit-learnPython’s main library for classical ML (imported as sklearn); it gives ready-made models and tools for splitting, scaling and scoring data.Note ML-012Train-test split
G-1751SciPyA Python library built on NumPy that adds more scientific routines, such as extra linear algebra and statistics functions.Note MA-047Linear algebra roadmap
G-1753ScoreIn naive Bayes, the likelihood times the prior for one class; it is not the probability of the class, only proportional to it, which is enough to pick the class with the largest score.Note ML-081Naive Bayes
G-1752Score functionIn attention, the rule that gives the raw score eij​ of how well encoder state j matches decoder step i; a softmax turns these scores into attention weights, and Bahdanau and Luong attention differ in this rule.Note DL-070Attention mechanism
G-1754Scott’s ruleA rule of thumb that picks a KDE’s bandwidth from the data’s standard deviation s and size n, s×n−1/5, so more data gives a narrower bandwidth; seaborn and SciPy use it by default.Note MA-023Kernel density estimation (KDE)
G-2205Scree plotA bar chart with one bar per principal component, showing its share of the total variance (eigenvalue ÷ sum of eigenvalues); it shows how many components are worth keeping.Note ML-047PCA
G-1755SDLCSoftware development life cycle: the standard sequence of steps for building a software product from start to end; the ML development life cycle adapts it to ML projects.Note ML-009ML development life cycle
G-1756Search spaceThe ranges or lists of values each hyperparameter may take during tuning; the tuner only tries values from it, and each added value multiplies the number of combinations.Note ML-128Bayesian optimisation
G-1757Secant equationThe condition Bk+1​s=y on the matrix that stands in for the Hessian: the new matrix must reproduce the gradient change y seen over the last step s, so it captures the curvature just observed.Note MA-064Hessian and multivariate Taylor
G-1758Secant lineA straight line through two points of a curve; as the second point slides towards the first, it turns into the tangent line, whose slope is the derivative.Note MA-061Derivatives of one variable
G-2249Second derivativeThe derivative of the derivative; it measures how the curve bends.Note MA-064Hessian and multivariate Taylor
G-2257Second derivative testA test that tells what a flat point (where f′=0) is from the sign of the second derivative: f′′>0 a local minimum, f′′<0 a local maximum, f′′=0 no conclusion.Note MA-067Hessian and multivariate Taylor
G-1759Second moment vt​In Adam, the running average (EWMA) of the squared gradient, an estimate of its mean square; dividing the step by vt​​ gives each weight its own step size, as in RMSProp.Note DL-038Adam
G-1760Second partial derivativeA partial derivative taken of a partial derivative, such as ∂2f/∂x2; it measures how the slope along one input changes, that is, how the surface bends.Note MA-064Hessian and multivariate Taylor
G-2253Second partial derivative testA test that tells what a stationary point of a function of two inputs is from one number, D=fxx​fyy​−fxy2​: D>0 a minimum or maximum (by the sign of fxx​), D<0 a saddle point, D=0 no answer.Note MA-064Hessian and multivariate Taylor
G-1761Second-order conditionA test of whether a function is bowl-shaped (convex) by its curvature: a twice-differentiable function is convex exactly when its Hessian is positive semi-definite everywhere (with one input, when f′′≥0 everywhere).Note MA-067Convex sets and convex optimisation
G-2157Selection biasThe optimism of a score that was picked as the best of many noisy scores: the winner partly won by luck on the same folds, so it looks a little better than it will on new data.Note ML-093Grid and random search
G-1762SelectKBestscikit-learn class that gives every column a score and keeps the k best, so only the most useful features go into the model.Note ML-028Feature selection
G-1763Self-attention (intra-attention)Attention in which the words of one sequence attend to each other (the queries, keys and values all come from that sequence); it gives each word a new vector that depends on the words around it.Note DL-077Self-attention (query, key, value)
G-1765Self-normalisingKeeping the activations of every layer at mean 0 and standard deviation 1 without a separate normalisation step.Note DL-028Leaky ReLU, PReLU, ELU and SELU
G-1766SELUScaled exponential linear unit: an activation that is ELU with α≈1.6733, multiplied by λ≈1.0507; these constants make a network self-normalising, keeping each layer’s outputs near mean 0 and standard deviation 1.Note DL-028Leaky ReLU, PReLU, ELU and SELU
G-1767SemesterOne of two six-month halves of a year.Note ML-033Date and time features
G-1768Semi-supervised learningLearning from a few labelled rows and many unlabelled ones: the algorithm labels the rest from the few labels, which saves the cost of labelling everything by hand.Note ML-003Semi-supervised learning
G-2275Sensitivity (of a model)How much a model’s prediction changes when its input changes a little; smaller weights make it lower, so the decision boundary is smoother.Note DL-026L1 and L2 regularisation in neural networks
G-1769Sentiment analysisDeciding whether a text expresses a positive or negative opinion.Note ML-008Applications of ML
G-1770SeparatorThe character between values on a line, such as , or a tab.Note ML-014CSV files
G-1771Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) modelA model whose input and output are both sequences, such as a translator from English to Hindi; in RNNs it is the many-to-many type.Note DL-058Sequence-to-sequence (encoder-decoder)
G-1772Sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) taskA task with a sequence as input and a sequence as output, possibly of different lengths, such as translation.Note DL-067Sequence-to-sequence (encoder-decoder)
G-1774Sequential dataData that comes as an ordered series of pieces whose order matters, such as text or a time series; models read it one piece after another, in order.Note DL-055Sequential data
G-1775Sequential learningTraining the base models one after another, each learning from the mistakes of the ones before; this is how boosting works.Note ML-113Boosting
G-1776Sequential modelA Keras model whose layers form one stack, each feeding the next.Note DL-011Keras workflow
G-1777Sequential trainingTraining in which step t must wait for step t−1, as in an RNN; it cannot be spread over many processors.Note DL-071Transformer
G-1778Seriespandas’ one-column structure: a list of values with an index; a DataFrame is several Series side by side.Note ML-014CSV files
G-1779ServerA computer that is always on and that users reach over the internet; a model runs on one so that other people can use it.Note ML-004Deployment
G-1780set_outputMethod that, called as set_output(transform="pandas"), makes a scikit-learn transformer return a pandas DataFrame with column names instead of a bare NumPy array.Note ML-027Column transformer
G-1781set_paramsMethod that changes a model’s settings after it is created.Note ML-105Random forest
G-1782SGDClassifierscikit-learn’s linear classifier that learns its weights by stochastic gradient descent (SGD), small steps from one row at a time, with a choice of loss (perceptron, log loss, hinge, …).Note DL-006Perceptron loss
G-1783SGDRegressorA scikit-learn model that does linear regression with stochastic gradient descent, step by step, so it can also learn from data arriving in small pieces.Note ML-005Online learning
G-1784Shadow priceThe Lagrange multiplier read in economic terms: how much the best value would improve per extra unit of a limited resource, so it tells how much loosening a constraint is worth.Note MA-066Lagrange multipliers, KKT and duality
G-1785Shallow decision treeA decision tree with a small maximum depth: high bias, low variance; boosting uses such trees as its base models.Note ML-113Boosting
G-1787ShapeThe number of items along each axis of a tensor, such as (2, 3) for a matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns; it tells how the data is laid out.Note ML-010Tensors
G-1786Shape ruleThe rule for which matrices can be multiplied: an m×n matrix times an n×p matrix gives an m×p matrix, so the inner sizes must match.Note MA-054Matrix multiplication as composition
G-1788Shapiro-Wilk testA statistical test of whether data follows a normal distribution: it takes the values and returns a statistic and a p-value, and a small p-value says the data is unlikely to be normal.Note MA-042T-tests: one-sample, two-sample, paired
G-1789ShearA linear transformation that keeps ^ fixed and slants ^​, so horizontal lines slide sideways, more the higher they are.Note MA-053Linear transformations and matrices
G-1790Shift rightPutting <start> in front of the target sentence to form the decoder’s input, so each position predicts the next word.Note DL-084Transformer decoder
G-1791ShiftingAdding or subtracting the same scalar to every component of a vector, such as [2,3]+1=[3,4]; it moves the point to a new place.Note MA-049Vector magnitude, distance and scalar operations
G-1792Short-term and long-term contributionsWhen an RNN learns, the signal that adjusts its weights (the BPTT gradient) is a sum of two kinds of parts: short-term ones measure how the loss changes through recent inputs, long-term ones through distant inputs. The long-term ones shrink towards 0, so the RNN fails to learn from distant inputs.Note DL-060Long-term dependency problem
G-1793Short-term contextWhat is happening in the sequence right now; an LSTM keeps it apart from the long-term context, which holds what matters for the whole sequence.Note DL-061LSTM (long short-term memory)
G-1794Shortcut variance formulaA quicker way to compute a variance: the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean, Var(X)=E[X2]−(E[X])2; it gives the same number as the definition.Note MA-012Expected value and variance of a random variable
G-1796ShrinkageThe pulling of a model’s coefficients towards 0 by a penalty, as when Ridge’s alpha grows; it makes the model rely less on any one feature and can reduce overfitting.Note ML-062Ridge regression
G-1795Shrinkage (boosting)Scaling down each base model’s contribution so the ensemble learns in small steps and overfits less.Note ML-112AdaBoost
G-1797ShufflingPutting the rows in a new random order before each epoch, so the mini-batches differ from one epoch to the next.Note ML-059Mini-batch gradient descent
G-1798Sigmoid functionAn S-shaped function that squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, σ(z)=1/(1+e−z); it turns a score into a probability, as in logistic regression.Note ML-071Sigmoid function
G-1799Sigmoid kernelA way to score how alike two points are, built from an S-shaped curve, tanh(γx⋅x′+r) (a kernel). Like other kernels, it lets an SVM draw a curved boundary without computing new features.Note ML-089Kernel trick
G-1800Sign functionReturns +1 for a positive number and -1 for a negative one; AdaBoost uses it to turn the weighted vote of its stumps into a class.Note ML-109AdaBoost
G-1801Significance level (α)The chance, fixed before the test, of wrongly declaring an effect when there is none (rejecting H0​ when it is actually true); usually 0.05.Note MA-039Hypothesis testing: null and alternative
G-2266SiLU (Swish)A smooth version of ReLU that multiplies each input by its sigmoid, zσ(z); it is used as an activation and is close to GELU. SiLU stands for sigmoid linear unit; it is also called Swish.Note DL-028Leaky ReLU, PReLU, ELU and SELU
G-1805SimilarityHow alike two data points are, measured as a distance: the closer two points are, the more similar; instance-based methods such as KNN use it to find the nearest examples.Note ML-006Instance-based learning
G-1802Similarity measureA number that says how alike two vectors are, such as the cosine similarity; ML uses it to compare data points or words.Note MA-050Cosine similarity
G-1804Similarity scoreA number that says how well the leftover errors (residuals) in one node of an XGBoost regression tree agree: (sum of residuals)2/(number of residuals+λ). The tree keeps the split that raises it the most.Note ML-118XGBoost
G-1803Similarity score (classification)The same score for XGBoost classification trees: how well the leftover errors (residuals) in a node agree, (sum of residuals)2/(∑p(1−p)+λ) with p the previous probabilities. As in regression, it is used to choose splits.Note ML-119XGBoost
G-1806Simple (elementary) eventAn event with exactly one outcome.Note MA-010Events and sample spaces
G-1807Simple cellA nerve cell in the brain’s first visual area (V1) that responds to an edge of one orientation at one place in a small patch of the view (its receptive field).Note DL-041Convolutional neural network (CNN)
G-1808Simple linear regressionLinear regression with one input column: it fits a straight line y=mx+b to predict the output from that one feature.Note ML-049Simple linear regression
G-1809SimpleImputerscikit-learn’s class that fills missing values, by default with the column’s mean.Note ML-027Simple imputation (mean, median, mode, constant)
G-2259Simplex algorithmA way to find the best corner of the region allowed by linear limits (solving a linear program): walk from one corner (vertex) to a neighbouring, better one until no neighbour is better.Note MA-068Linear and quadratic programming
G-1810Simulated annealingAn optimisation method named after slowly cooling metal, which then settles into a stable, low-energy state: it lowers a temperature step by step so the search settles down; a learning schedule that lowers the learning rate resembles it.Note ML-058Stochastic gradient descent
G-1811Single linkageIn hierarchical clustering, a way to measure the distance between two clusters: the distance of their closest pair of points; the two closest clusters are merged next.Note ML-125Hierarchical clustering
G-1812Singular value (σi​)A stretch factor of a matrix: the length of Avi​; never negative, listed largest first.Note MA-057Singular value decomposition
G-1813Singular value decomposition (SVD)A way to write any matrix, square or not, as three simple steps: turn, stretch by the singular values, turn (A=UΣVT: orthogonal, diagonal, orthogonal; a factorisation). ML uses it for PCA and to compress data.Note MA-057Singular value decomposition
G-1814Singular value equationThe equation Avi​=σi​ui​: the matrix sends each input direction vi​ to its output direction ui​, stretched by the singular value σi​; it is used to compute each ui​.Note MA-057Singular value decomposition
G-1815Sinusoidal positional encodingThe fixed position code of the original transformer (Vaswani et al.): each position gets a vector of sine waves (even dimensions) and cosine waves (odd dimensions) of different wavelengths, added to the word’s embedding so the model knows word order.Note DL-079Positional encoding
G-1816SizeThe total number of items in an array: the numbers in its shape multiplied together.Note ML-010Tensors
G-1817SkewnessA number for how lopsided a distribution is: 0 symmetric, positive right tail, negative left tail.Note ML-019Skewness
G-1819Skip connection through timeA connection from a hidden state several steps back directly to the present; it gives the gradient a shorter path, so it vanishes less.Note DL-060Long-term dependency problem
G-1820Slack (ξ)A number for each training point in the soft-margin SVM that says how far the point lies on the wrong side of its own margin line, in margin units: 0 on the correct side, above 1 on the wrong side of π (slack ξi​). The loss adds up the slacks, so each violation has a cost.Note ML-088Hinge loss and soft margin
G-1821Slater’s conditionThere is at least one point that meets every inequality limit with room to spare (strictly). Together with convexity, this guarantees that the related helper (dual) problem gives the same best value as the original (strong duality).Note MA-067Convex sets and convex optimisation
G-1822slice(0, 10)Python object meaning positions 0 up to, not including, 10.Note ML-028ML pipelines
G-1823SlopeHow much the output changes for one unit of change in the input; m in y=mx+b.Note ML-049Simple linear regression
G-1824Slow convergenceReaching a good solution only after very many epochs.Note DL-029Weight initialisation
G-1825SMOTESynthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique: it grows the minority class until the classes are equal by making new rows on the line between a minority row and one of its minority neighbours.Note ML-127SMOTE
G-1826Soft assignmentSharing a point among clusters by probabilities instead of giving it to one.Note MA-073Gaussian mixture model (GMM)
G-1827Soft thresholdingMoving a value towards 0 by a fixed amount, and setting it to 0 if it would cross 0; this is how Lasso sets coefficients to exactly 0.Note ML-067Lasso regression
G-1828Soft votingPredicting the class with the highest average predicted probability across the base models.Note ML-097Voting ensembles
G-1829Soft-margin SVMThe SVM that allows points inside the margin or on the wrong side, at a cost controlled by C.Note ML-088Hinge loss and soft margin
G-1830Softmax functionA function that turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1: raise e to each score and divide by the total, ezk​/∑j​ezj​; it gives one probability per class in multi-class models.Note ML-078Softmax regression
G-1831Softmax gradientHow much each softmax output changes when one input score changes: ∂αi​/∂si​=αi​(1−αi​) and ∂αi​/∂sj​=−αi​αj​; training changes the scores through it, and it is near 0 everywhere when the softmax is saturated.Note DL-075Scaled dot-product attention
G-1832Softmax output layerAn output layer with one node per class whose outputs are probabilities adding up to 1.Note DL-012ANN for classification
G-1833Softmax regressionLogistic regression extended to any number of classes using the softmax function.Note ML-078Softmax regression
G-1834SoftplusA smooth curve, ln(1+ez), that bends upward (convex) and whose slope at every point is the sigmoid.Note MA-067Convex and non-convex loss
G-1835Software integrationBuilding a model into the software that users use.Note ML-007Software integration
G-1836SolverThe method a model uses to find its best settings during training.Note ML-080Logistic regression
G-1837Spam classifierA program that decides whether an email is spam or not.Note ML-001Machine learning
G-1838SpanThe set of all linear combinations of some vectors: every point reachable by scaling and adding them, such as the whole plane for ^ and ^​.Note MA-052Linear combinations, span and basis
G-1846SparseMostly made of zeros, such as a feature map whose values are almost all 0, or a model whose coefficients are mostly exactly 0.Note DL-052Visualising what a CNN learns
G-1839Sparse categorical cross-entropyThe same loss as categorical cross-entropy, but it takes the labels as plain integers (such as the digits 0 to 9) instead of one-hot vectors, so the labels need no encoding.Note DL-012Categorical and sparse categorical cross-entropy
G-1840Sparse dataTwo senses: a table that is mostly zeros (as after one-hot encoding); or, in many dimensions, a space where most regions hold no points.Note ML-024Normalization
G-1841Sparse featureA feature whose values are mostly zero, such as “studied at an IIT”.Note DL-036AdaGrad
G-1842Sparse interactionsEach output of a convolution depends only on a small window of the input, because the filter is small; so a convolution needs far fewer weights than a fully connected layer.Note DL-046Convolutional neural network (CNN)
G-1843Sparse matrixA table stored as only its non-zero entries, to save memory.Note ML-026One-hot encoding
G-1844Sparse modelA model in which many coefficients are exactly 0; those features have no effect and can be dropped, so the model also does feature selection.Note ML-066Lasso regression
G-1845Sparse representationA representation where most values are 0, such as a one-hot vector over a 10,000-word vocabulary (9,999 zeros and one 1); it wastes space compared with a dense one.Note DL-057Word embeddings
G-1847sparse_outputThe OneHotEncoder setting that picks the output format: False returns a normal NumPy array instead of a sparse matrix (a table stored as only its non-zero entries).Note ML-026One-hot encoding
G-1849SparsityHaving many coefficients exactly equal to 0.Note ML-067Lasso regression
G-1848Sparsity SThe probability that a feature is 0 in an observation; high sparsity means the feature is rarely active.Note DL-090Superposition and nearly perpendicular directions
G-1850Sparsity-aware split findingXGBoost’s way of handling missing values: at each split it tries sending them to the left and to the right side and keeps the side with the higher gain.Note ML-117XGBoost
G-1851Spatial arrangementWhere each pixel sits relative to the others; an ANN that flattens the image loses it, while a CNN’s filters use it by looking at neighbouring pixels.Note DL-040Convolutional neural network (CNN)
G-2209SpecificityOf all items that really are negative, the fraction the model cleared: TN / (TN + FP).Note ML-076Precision, recall and F1
G-1852Spectral normThe largest stretch a matrix gives to any input of length 1, ∥M∥2​=σ1​; it is one way to measure the size of a matrix.Note MA-059Low-rank approximation (truncated SVD)
G-1853splitterA decision tree setting for how each split’s threshold is chosen: “best” searches every threshold, “random” draws thresholds at random, which adds randomness that pays off when many trees are averaged.Note ML-092Decision trees
G-1855SplittingDividing a node’s rows into parts according to a question.Note ML-091Decision trees
G-1854Splitting criterion (threshold)The value a numerical question in a decision tree compares against, such as petal length ≤ 2.45; the tree keeps the threshold with the highest information gain.Note ML-091Decision trees
G-1856SpyderA Python code editor that shows variables and tables in memory.Note ML-011Setup: conda, Jupyter and Colab
G-1857SQL (Structured Query Language)The language for asking a database for data.Note ML-015JSON and SQL data
G-1858SQLAlchemyA Python library that connects to many kinds of database; pandas supports it fully.Note ML-015JSON and SQL data
G-1859SQLiteA database stored in a single file, built into Python, needing no server.Note ML-015JSON and SQL data
G-1860Square root transformReplacing each value with x​; it pulls a right tail in, more gently than the log.Note ML-029Function transformer
G-1861Square transformReplacing each value with x2; used for left-skewed data.Note ML-029Function transformer
G-1862Square-root ruleA rough starting value for k, the number of neighbours in KNN: about n​, where n is the number of training rows, made odd to avoid ties.Note ML-085K-nearest neighbours
G-1863Squared loss (L2 loss)The squared difference between target and prediction, (y−y^​)2, used as the error a model lowers during training, so large errors cost much more than small ones; averaged over the rows it is the mean squared error.Note DL-014Loss functions in deep learning
G-1864squared_errorThe default rule DecisionTreeRegressor uses to judge splits: it splits by mean squared error, and each leaf predicts the mean of its rows.Note ML-093Regression trees
G-1865Stacked (deep) LSTMSeveral LSTM layers on top of each other, each feeding its outputs to the next; the extra layers give the model more room and capacity, with higher layers working closer to the meaning.Note DL-068Deep (stacked) RNNs
G-1866StackingAn ensemble in which the base models’ predictions become the input columns of a new dataset, and a final meta-model learns how best to combine them.Note ML-121Stacking and blending
G-1867Stage-wise additive modelA model built as a sum of base models added one at a time, one per stage; boosting builds this kind of model, each new part learning from the mistakes of the ones before.Note ML-109Boosting
G-1868staged_scoreA method that gives an ensemble’s score after each added stage.Note ML-112Gradient boosting
G-1869Standard basis (^, ^​)The unit vectors along the axes, [1,0] and [0,1] in 2D; every vector is a sum of scaled copies of them, and its coordinates are those scales.Note MA-052Linear combinations, span and basis
G-1871Standard deviationHow far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n−1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default).Note ML-018Variance
G-1870Standard deviation of a random variableThe square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value.Note MA-012Expected value and variance of a random variable
G-1872Standard errorHow much a statistic, such as the sample mean, changes from one sample to the next, so how precise it is as an estimate. It is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution; for the mean, σ/n​.Note MA-033Sampling distribution and standard error
G-1873Standard normal distributionThe normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, written Z∼N(0,1); any normal variable can be converted to it with z-scores, so one table of probabilities serves every normal distribution.Note MA-025Standard normal and the z-table
G-1874StandardizationScaling a column to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation), so features measured on different scales become comparable.Note ML-023Standardization
G-1875standardizeThe PowerTransformer parameter (on by default) that rescales the output to mean 0 and standard deviation 1.Note ML-030Power transformer
G-1876StandardScalerscikit-learn’s class that standardizes columns: fit learns each column’s mean and standard deviation from the training set, and transform applies (x−xˉ)/σ.Note ML-023Standardization
G-1877Static embeddingAn embedding that gives a word the same vector in every sentence, so “bank” gets one vector in both “money bank” and “river bank”; self-attention fixes this by making the vector depend on context.Note DL-073Contextual embeddings
G-1878Static modelA model that learns nothing new after deployment.Note ML-004Batch (offline) learning
G-1879Stationary pointA point where a function is flat, its slope is zero (the derivative, or every partial derivative, is zero); it is a minimum, a maximum or a saddle point.Note MA-065Convex and non-convex loss
G-1880StatisticA number computed from a sample, such as the sample mean xˉ; it is used as an estimate of the matching number for the whole population (a parameter).Note MA-004Population, sample, parameter and statistic
G-1881Statistical hypothesis testA method that uses sample data to decide whether a claim about a whole population (a hypothesis about a population parameter) is supported strongly enough; it is a form of statistical inference.Note MA-038Hypothesis testing: null and alternative
G-1882Statistical momentsAverages of distances from the mean raised to a power: mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis.Note MA-028Kurtosis and moments
G-1884StatisticsThe branch of mathematics for collecting, analysing, interpreting and presenting data.Note MA-004Inferential statistics
G-1885statsmodelsA Python library for statistical models and tests, such as the VIF and the Durbin-Watson statistic used to check the assumptions of linear regression.Note ML-055Assumptions of linear regression
G-1886Status codeA number saying how a request went: 200 OK, 401, 404, 500.Note ML-016APIs
G-1887Status quoAnother name for the null hypothesis H0​: the current state of things, which the test keeps unless the data gives strong evidence against it.Note MA-038Hypothesis testing: null and alternative
G-1888Steepest ascentThe direction in which f increases fastest: the direction of the gradient; gradient descent steps the opposite way to go downhill fastest.Note MA-062Partial derivatives and gradients
G-1889Step functionA function that outputs 1 for positive inputs and 0 otherwise; the classic perceptron uses it to turn its score into a class.Note ML-069Perceptron
G-1893StochasticInvolving randomness, as in stochastic gradient descent, which picks rows at random.Note ML-058Stochastic gradient descent
G-1891Stochastic errorA random, unmeasurable influence that scatters data around its trend.Note ML-049Simple linear regression
G-1892Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)Gradient descent that uses one random row for every update, so each update is cheap and many updates happen per epoch, at the cost of a noisier path.Note ML-058Stochastic gradient descent
G-1894Stopping ruleThe condition that ends a training loop: a fixed number of loops, or convergence.Note DL-005Perceptron
G-1895str dtypeThe pandas 3 type for text columns, replacing object.Note ML-032Mixed variables
G-1896str.extractThe pandas method that returns the part of each value matching a regular expression.Note ML-032Mixed variables
G-1897Strength of a relationshipHow closely the points follow a straight line; measured by ∣r∣.Note MA-009Covariance and covariance matrix
G-1898Strength of evidenceHow strongly the data speaks against the starting claim of no effect (H0​); the rejection region approach does not measure it.Note MA-039Z-test and rejection regions
G-1899Strictly convex functionA function whose curve lies strictly below the straight line (chord) joining any two different points of it; it has at most one minimum.Note MA-065Convex and non-convex loss
G-1900StrideThe number of pixels the filter moves at each step; a stride larger than 1 makes the output smaller.Note DL-043Padding and strides
G-1901Strided convolutionA convolution with a stride larger than 1, used to make the feature map smaller.Note DL-043Padding and strides
G-1902Strike rateA batter’s runs per 100 balls faced.Note ML-044Feature construction and splitting
G-1903Strong dualityThe best lower bound given by a related helper problem (the dual problem) equals the true minimum of the original (primal) problem, so solving the dual solves the original; it holds for convex problems.Note MA-066Lagrange multipliers, KKT and duality
G-1904Strong learnerA model with high accuracy.Note ML-109Boosting
G-1905Structure scoreXGBoost’s number for how good one tree’s shape is: the best value of its loss-plus-penalty objective, −21​∑j​Gj2​/(Hj​+λ)+γT. Lower is better, so it is used to compare candidate splits.Note ML-120XGBoost
G-1906Student’s t-distributionA bell-shaped distribution like the standard normal but with fatter tails. It is used in place of the standard normal when the population’s σ is unknown and estimated by the sample’s s; it is the distribution of (Xˉ−μ)/(s/n​) and approaches the standard normal as n grows.Note MA-037Student’s t-distribution
G-1907StudyIn Optuna, one full search for the best settings: a collection of trials, each scoring one set of values, aimed at optimising the objective function.Note ML-128Optuna
G-1908Sub-layerOne of the two parts of an encoder block: multi-head attention or the feed-forward network.Note DL-081Transformer encoder
G-1909Sub-networkThe smaller network left after dropout switches some nodes off; it shares the full network’s weights, and each training step trains a different one.Note DL-024Dropout
G-1910SubgradientA slope used at a corner of a function, where the ordinary derivative does not exist.Note DL-006Perceptron loss
G-1911SubscriptionA model where customers pay a fixed amount every month (or year).Note ML-013Framing an ML problem
G-1914Sum of squares (SST, SSB, SSW)The squared distances from a mean added up, before dividing: total (SST), between-group (SSB) and within-group (SSW), with SST=SSB+SSW; ANOVA compares the between-group and within-group parts to test whether group means differ.Note MA-046One-way ANOVA
G-1915Summation (z)The weighted sum w1​x1​+w2​x2​+⋯+b inside a perceptron.Note DL-004Perceptron
G-1917SuperpositionA network storing more features than it has dimensions by giving each feature its own nearly perpendicular direction.Note DL-090Superposition and nearly perpendicular directions
G-1916Superposition hypothesisThe proposal that real neural networks store features in superposition (Elhage et al. 2022).Note DL-090Superposition and nearly perpendicular directions
G-1918Supervised binningGrouping a column’s values into ranges (binning) with edges chosen using the target too, such as decision tree binning.Note ML-031Binning and binarization
G-1919Supervised learningLearning from data with inputs and outputs, to predict outputs.Note ML-003Supervised learning
G-1920SupervisionCorrect answers that guide an algorithm while it learns.Note ML-003Supervised learning
G-1924SupportThe number of items that really belong to a class.Note ML-076Precision, recall and F1
G-1921Support vector machine (SVM)A classifier that separates the classes with the line, or flat surface in more dimensions (a hyperplane), that leaves the widest gap (margin) between the classes.Note ML-086Support vector machines
G-1922Support vector regression (SVR)The regression version of SVM: the same ideas, used to predict a number instead of a class.Note ML-086Support vector machines
G-1923Support vectorsThe training points that lie on the two margin lines, π+ or π−; they alone fix the SVM line.Note ML-086Support vector machines
G-1925Sure (certain) eventThe event that contains every outcome, the whole sample space, so it always happens; its probability is 1.Note MA-010Events and sample spaces
G-1926Surge pricingRaising fares when demand is much higher than supply.Note ML-008Applications of ML
G-2221SurpriseHow unexpected a class is: log2​(1/p) for a class with share p; entropy is the average surprise.Note ML-091Entropy, information gain and Gini
G-1927Surrogate modelA cheap stand-in for the unknown score function, built by Bayesian optimisation from the trials so far; it is used to guess which hyperparameter values to try next.Note ML-128Bayesian optimisation
G-1928Survival functionThe probability of a value above x: one minus the CDF; sf in scipy.Note MA-031Bernoulli and binomial distributions
G-1930SwitchesThe stored positions of the largest values that max pooling kept; max pooling’s backward pass needs them.Note DL-048Backpropagation in a CNN
G-1931Symbolic AIEarly AI where humans write the knowledge as rules.Note ML-002Symbolic AI and expert systems
G-1932Symmetric matrixA square matrix equal to its own transpose, such as XTX or a covariance matrix; it always has a full set of perpendicular eigenvectors.Note MA-057Singular value decomposition
G-1933Symmetry problemNodes that start with equal weights get equal updates and stay identical, so a layer acts like one node.Note DL-029Weight initialisation
G-1934Synthetic dataRows created by an algorithm rather than collected.Note ML-127Random under- and oversampling
G-1935System promptText placed before the user’s message that sets the scene for a chatbot.Note DL-087Decoder-only GPT
G-1936T critical valueThe cut-off from Student’s t-distribution that leaves α/2 in each tail; the t-interval multiplies the standard error by it in place of zα/2​. For 95% and n=30 it is 2.045.Note MA-037Student’s t-distribution
G-1937T statisticThe number a t-test computes from the sample: how many estimated standard errors (s/n​) the sample mean lies from the mean claimed by H0​; the test decides from its size.Note MA-042T-tests: one-sample, two-sample, paired
G-1938T-procedureThe way to build a confidence interval for a mean when the population standard deviation σ is unknown: use the sample’s s and a t critical value in place of z, giving xˉ±tα/2,n−1​s/n​.Note MA-037Student’s t-distribution
G-1939T-tableA table of t critical values with one row per degrees of freedom and one column per tail area; we read the cut-off for a t-interval or t-test from it.Note MA-037Student’s t-distribution
G-1940T-testA hypothesis test about means that uses the sample standard deviation and Student’s t-distribution.Note MA-042T-tests: one-sample, two-sample, paired
G-1941TagOne labelled box of a web page in HTML, such as a heading or a paragraph (<h2>TCS</h2>); a scraper finds the values it wants by their tags.Note ML-017Web scraping
G-1942Tail (of a distribution)The part of the curve far from the centre, where values are rare.Note ML-041Z-score outlier method
G-1943Tail eventAn event with a very low probability but a very large effect.Note MA-026Skewness
G-1944TailednessHow much probability lies far from the mean, in the tails.Note MA-028Kurtosis and moments
G-1945Tangent lineThe line that touches a curve at one point with the curve’s slope there; the limit of secant lines.Note MA-061Derivatives of one variable
G-1946Tangent planeThe flat plane that touches a surface at one point with the same slopes (gradient) there; it approximates the surface near that point and is the first-order Taylor approximation.Note MA-064Hessian and multivariate Taylor
G-1947Tanh (hyperbolic tangent)An activation function that squashes any number into an S-curve from −1 to 1, centred on 0: tanh(z)=(ez−e−z)/(ez+e−z), with derivative 1−tanh2(z).Note DL-027Tanh
G-1949TargetThe output column we predict, such as the class; also called the label.Note ML-003Supervised learning
G-2185Target encodingReplacing each category by the mean of the target for that category, learned on training rows only.Note ML-026Encoding categorical data
G-1948Target leakageBuilding an input column from the answer itself, so the model sees information it would not have in real use.Note ML-051Data leakage
G-1951Targeted marketingAdvertising only to the people most likely to buy.Note ML-008Applications of ML
G-1952Task-specific contextual embeddingA contextual embedding (a word’s vector built from its neighbouring words) whose way of mixing the neighbours is learned from the task’s data, so a phrase such as “piece of cake” gets the meaning the task needs.Note DL-074Self-attention (query, key, value)
G-1953Taylor polynomialA polynomial built from a function’s value and its first n derivatives at one point x0​, used to approximate the function near x0​; it is the Taylor series cut after the (x−x0​)n term.Note MA-061Taylor series
G-1954Taylor seriesApproximation of a function near a point by a polynomial built from its derivatives there.Note ML-120XGBoost
G-1955Teacher forcingFeeding the correct (gold) previous token to the decoder during training instead of its own prediction, so every step learns from a correct history and training goes faster.Note DL-068Teacher forcing
G-1956Temperature TA number that makes a model’s probabilities sharper or flatter: every raw score (logit) is divided by it before the softmax; low T sharpens, high T flattens.Note DL-088Unembedding, logits, temperature and sampling
G-1957TensorA container of numbers arranged along one or more axes.Note ML-010Tensors
G-1959TensorFlowGoogle’s deep learning library for building and training neural networks; most code in these Notes uses it with Keras, its built-in high-level interface.Note DL-001Keras workflow
G-1958TensorFlow PlaygroundA website that trains small neural networks in the browser and shows their boundaries.Note DL-007Problem with the perceptron (XOR)
G-1960Terminal regionThe part of the input space that ends in one leaf of a tree, written Rjm​ for leaf j of tree m; every point in it gets that leaf’s output.Note ML-115Gradient boosting
G-1961Terminal velocityThe step size momentum reaches when every gradient is the same: ηg/(1−β).Note DL-034SGD with momentum
G-2211Test accuracyAccuracy on data not used for training, an estimate of performance on new data.Note ML-079Logistic regression
G-1962Test setThe part hidden during training, used to check the model.Note ML-012Train-test split
G-1963Test statisticThe number a test computes from the sample to make its decision, such as z or t.Note MA-038Hypothesis testing: null and alternative
G-1964Text generatorA next-word predictor run in a loop, each predicted word added to the text.Note DL-063Next-word prediction with an LSTM
G-1966Theoretical (classical) probabilityFavourable outcomes divided by all outcomes, for equally likely outcomes.Note MA-011Empirical vs theoretical probability, probability rules
G-1967Theoretical distributionThe known distribution that data is compared with, for example on a Q-Q plot.Note MA-028Q-Q plot
G-1968Theoretical quantileWhere a value would sit if the data were perfectly normal (the horizontal axis of a Q-Q plot).Note ML-029Q-Q plot
G-1969Thin (reduced) SVDA smaller form of the SVD that drops the columns of U multiplied by the zero rows of Σ; those columns never affect the matrix, so it gives the same A from smaller matrices.Note MA-057Singular value decomposition
G-1971Threshold (binarization)The value that separates 0 from 1 in binarization.Note ML-031Binning and binarization
G-1970Threshold (classification)The probability above which a prediction counts as class 1.Note DL-011ANN for classification
G-2261Threshold (of a perceptron)The value the weighted sum must reach for the output to be 1; it equals −b.Note DL-004Perceptron
G-1972Tidy dataData laid out with one record (observation) per row and one single value per cell.Note ML-044Feature construction and splitting
G-1973Tied weightsUsing one matrix for two jobs: the token embedding matrix turns tokens into vectors at the input, and the same matrix turns the final vector back into one score per token at the output.Note DL-087Decoder-only GPT
G-1974Time axis and depth axisThe two directions of an unfolded deep RNN: time steps and layers.Note DL-065Deep (stacked) RNNs
G-1975Time seriesData recorded at regular time intervals.Note ML-010Tensors
G-1976Time stepOne position in the sequence; word j enters at t=j.Note DL-056Recurrent neural network (RNN)
G-1977TimedeltaA length of time, the result of subtracting two datetimes.Note ML-033Date and time features
G-1978Timestamppandas’ type for a single point in time.Note ML-033Date and time features
G-1979TitleThe word before a name, such as Mr, Mrs, Miss or Master.Note ML-044Feature construction and splitting
G-1981TokenOne unit of text the model reads or writes; here, one word.Note DL-087Decoder-only GPT
G-1980Token embedding matrix WE​The learned table with one vector per token (50,257 vectors of 768 numbers in GPT-2); in GPT-2 also used as the output matrix.Note DL-087Decoder-only GPT
G-1983Tokenisation (tokenization)Splitting a text into tokens (words or word pieces), the units a language model reads and writes, before they are turned into vectors.Note DL-081Tokenization and integer encoding of text
G-1988TopThe dense layers at the end of a CNN, which turn features into classes.Note DL-053Transfer learning (feature extraction and fine-tuning)
G-1985Top k samplingA sampling rule that keeps only the k most likely tokens and samples the next token among them, so very unlikely tokens are never picked.Note DL-088Unembedding, logits, temperature and sampling
G-1986Top activationsThe photos (or patches) that give a feature map its largest values.Note DL-052Visualising what a CNN learns
G-1987Top categoriesKeeping only the most frequent categories and merging the rest into one “uncommon” category.Note ML-026One-hot encoding
G-1989Top-1 errorThe share of photos whose true class is not the model’s single most likely class.Note DL-051Pretrained models and ImageNet
G-1990Top-5 errorThe share of photos whose true class is not among the model’s five most likely classes.Note DL-051Pretrained models and ImageNet
G-1991TopologyThe pattern of connections between a network’s layers.Note DL-054Keras functional API
G-1992Total responsibility Nk​About how many points one component k of a mixture accounts for: the sum, over all points, of that component’s share of each point (its responsibility).Note MA-073Gaussian mixture model (GMM)
G-1993Total sum of squaresThe total squared error of always predicting the mean yˉ​; R² compares the model’s error with this baseline.Note ML-051Regression metrics
G-1994Toy model of superpositionA tiny network that squeezes more features than it has hidden numbers and is trained to rebuild its input, x′=ReLU(WTWx+b); it shows when a network stores more features than dimensions (superposition).Note DL-090Superposition and nearly perpendicular directions
G-1995TPEOptuna’s default way to pick the hyperparameter values to try next from the results of past trials (its sampler, a form of Bayesian optimisation); TPE stands for Tree-structured Parzen Estimator.Note ML-128Optuna
G-1996TPUGoogle’s chip built only for deep learning maths.Note ML-011Setup: conda, Jupyter and Colab
G-1998Train-test splitDividing the data into a training set the model learns from and a test set held back to check it on unseen rows; it comes before scaling or fitting.Note ML-023Train-test split
G-2000Training (a perceptron)Finding its weights and bias from labelled data.Note DL-005Perceptron
G-1255Training (model training)Giving data to an algorithm so it learns the pattern: the model makes predictions, measures its errors and adjusts to reduce them.Note ML-009ML development life cycle
G-2001Training curves (learning curves)Loss or accuracy plotted against the epoch, for the training and validation sets; they show how the model improves as training goes on and when the two sets start to differ.Note DL-011Training curves (History)
G-2002Training setThe part of the data the model learns from.Note ML-012Train-test split
G-2004Transfer functionAnother name for the activation function: the function a node applies to its weighted sum to give its output.Note DL-027Activation functions
G-2005Transfer learningReusing a network trained by others on a big dataset for our own problem.Note DL-002Transfer learning (feature extraction and fine-tuning)
G-2006TransformationA function that takes a vector in and gives a vector out.Note MA-053Linear transformations and matrices
G-2007TransformerA neural network that turns one sequence into another (a seq2seq architecture) built from attention and dense layers, with no RNN, that processes all words in parallel.Note DL-067Transformer
G-2008transformersThe ColumnTransformer parameter that says which transformer to apply to which columns: a list of (name, transformer, columns) tuples.Note ML-027Column transformer
G-2009transformers_The attribute of a fitted column transformer that lists its fitted (name, transformer, columns) tuples; we use it to pull out one fitted step.Note ML-028Column transformer
G-2010Translation equivarianceThe output shifts in the same way as the input; a property of convolution.Note DL-044Pooling
G-2011Translation invarianceThe output stays (almost) the same when the input is shifted slightly.Note DL-044Pooling
G-2012TransposeA matrix or vector with rows and columns swapped; it turns a column vector u into a row uT, so uTx is the dot product.Note ML-053Normal equation
G-2013Tree-based algorithmAn algorithm that splits the data with simple conditions; hardly affected by outliers.Note ML-037Outliers
G-2014Tree-level feature sampling (tree-level column sampling)Drawing one random set of features per tree, before the tree is grown; every split of that tree uses only those features (bagging).Note ML-104Random forest
G-2016Trial (hyperparameter tuning)One run of a tuner (Optuna, Keras Tuner) with one set of hyperparameter values: one model built, trained and scored.Note ML-128Optuna
G-2015Trial (probability)One run of a random experiment; it gives exactly one outcome.Note MA-010Events and sample spaces
G-2017Trimmed meanThe mean after removing a fixed share of the smallest and largest values.Note MA-005Measures of central tendency
G-2019TrimmingRemoving the rows that hold outliers.Note ML-040Trimming outliers
G-2018Trimming percentageThe share of values removed from each end for a trimmed mean.Note MA-005Measures of central tendency
G-2020True negative (TN)A case the model predicts as negative that really is negative: a correct “no”. The count of these is one cell of the confusion matrix.Note ML-075Confusion matrix
G-2021True positive (TP)A case the model predicts as positive that really is positive: a correct “yes”. The count of these is one cell of the confusion matrix.Note ML-075Confusion matrix
G-2022True positive rate (TPR)The fraction of real positives the model flags; the same as recall.Note ML-077ROC curve and AUC
G-2023Truncated normalA normal distribution restricted to a range and rescaled so its area is 1; it keeps its bell shape inside the range. Keras’ normal initialisers cut at two standard deviations: values beyond are redrawn.Note DL-030Xavier and He initialisation
G-2024TruncatedSVDscikit-learn’s tool that cuts a matrix down to k columns by keeping only its top k singular directions (a rank k SVD); it does not centre the data, so it works on sparse matrices.Note MA-060Latent semantic analysis
G-2025TSV fileLike a CSV file, with tabs between values.Note ML-014CSV files
G-2026Tukey’s HSDA follow-up test (post-hoc test) that compares every pair of groups while keeping the overall chance of a false alarm (Type I error) at α.Note MA-046One-way ANOVA
G-2027Two-tailed p-valueThe p-value of a two-tailed test: the chance, if H0​ is true, of a test statistic at least as far from 0 as ours in either direction; for a z-test it is 2Φ(−∣z∣).Note MA-041P-values
G-2028Two-tailed test (two-sided test)A test that looks for an effect in either direction: H1​ uses =, and the significance level is split into α/2 in each tail.Note MA-040Type I and II errors, power, tails
G-2029Two-way ANOVAA test of whether each of two category columns changes the mean of a number column, and whether their combination (interaction) does; it is ANOVA with one numerical and two categorical columns.Note MA-044One-way ANOVA
G-2030Type 1 mixed variableA column whose cells each contain a category and a number together, such as C85.Note ML-032Mixed variables
G-2031Type 2 mixed variableA column with a number in some rows and a category in others.Note ML-032Mixed variables
G-2032Type I error (false positive)A false alarm: the test declares an effect when there is none (rejecting H0​ when it is actually true); its probability is α.Note MA-040Type I and II errors, power, tails
G-2033Type II error (false negative)A miss: the test finds no effect when there really is one (failing to reject H0​ when it is actually false); its probability is β.Note MA-040Type I and II errors, power, tails
G-2034Unbiased estimatorA formula that guesses a true value from a sample (an estimator) and is right on average: its average over many samples equals the true value.Note MA-071Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)
G-2035UnderfittingBeing too simple to capture the pattern; fails on all data.Note ML-007Underfitting
G-2036UnderflowA number too close to 0 for the computer to store, which then becomes 0 or loses precision.Note ML-072Logistic regression
G-2037Underlying distributionThe distribution that produced the data points.Note MA-023Density estimation
G-2038Understanding the dataThe project stage where we learn what is in the data before cleaning or modelling.Note ML-018Exploratory data analysis
G-2040UnembeddingThe last step of a language model: the final vector’s dot product with every token’s vector, one score per token.Note DL-088Unembedding, logits, temperature and sampling
G-2039Unembedding matrix WU​The matrix that turns a language model’s final vector into one score (logit) per vocabulary token; in GPT-2 it is the token embedding matrix WE​ itself (tied weights).Note DL-088Unembedding, logits, temperature and sampling
G-2041Unfolding (unrolling)Drawing the recurrent layer once per time step, so the loop becomes a chain.Note DL-056Recurrent neural network (RNN)
G-2042Unidirectional RNNAn RNN that reads in one direction only, so its output at t depends only on inputs up to t.Note DL-066Bidirectional RNNs
G-2043Uniform distributionA distribution in which every outcome in a range is equally likely.Note MA-029Uniform distribution
G-2044Uniform weightingEvery neighbour counts equally: the fill is their plain mean.Note ML-038KNN imputer
G-2045Union (A ∪ B)The set of elements in A or B (or both), such as the points inside either of two convex pieces of an obstacle; for events, the event that A or B (or both) happens.Note MA-017Empirical vs theoretical probability, probability rules
G-2046Unit hypercubeThe box from 0 to 1 along every axis in three or more dimensions (a unit cube in three); min-max scaling presses data with many columns into it.Note ML-024Normalization
G-2047Unit squareThe square from (0, 0) to (1, 1), into which min-max scaling presses two columns.Note ML-024Normalization
G-2048Unit vectorA vector of length 1, used to describe a direction.Note ML-047Vector magnitude, distance and scalar operations
G-2049UnitsThe LSTM setting for how many nodes each of its four internal layers has; it is also the length of the cell state ct​, the hidden state ht​ and every gate vector.Note DL-062LSTM gates (forget, input, output) and cell state
G-2050Univariate analysisStudying one column (variable) on its own, mostly with graphs, to see its values and spread; the column’s type decides which graphs to draw.Note ML-019Univariate analysis
G-2051Univariate imputationFilling the gaps in a column (imputation) using only that column’s other values.Note ML-034Missing values
G-2052Universal approximation theoremA network with a hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any continuous function.Note DL-003Universal approximation theorem
G-2053Universal set (U)The rectangle of a Venn diagram; in probability, the sample space, with P(U)=1.Note MA-013Venn diagrams and contingency tables
G-2054Unpaired t-testAnother name for the independent two-sample t-test: a t-test that compares the means of two separate groups whose values are not paired.Note MA-043T-tests: one-sample, two-sample, paired
G-2055Unreasonable effectiveness of dataWith enough data, different algorithms perform about the same.Note ML-007Enough data
G-2156Unstable modelA model whose fit changes a lot when the training data changes a little; bagging helps it most.Note ML-100Bagging
G-2056Unstable trainingTraining that does not progress because exploding gradients make the updates huge.Note DL-060Long-term dependency problem
G-2057Unsupervised binningBinning (grouping a column’s values into ranges) that sets the bin edges from the column’s own values only, without using the target.Note ML-031Binning and binarization
G-2058Unsupervised learningLearning from inputs only, to find structure.Note ML-003Unsupervised learning
G-2059Unsupervised pre-trainingSetting a network’s starting weights with a network trained layer by layer, instead of at random.Note DL-003Types of neural networks
G-2060Update gate (zt​)In a GRU, numbers between 0 and 1, the output of a sigmoid layer, that decide entry by entry how much of the new candidate memory replaces the old memory.Note DL-064GRU (gated recurrent unit)
G-2061Updates per epochHow many times the weights are updated in one pass over the data: one update per batch, so ⌈n/batch size⌉.Note DL-020Batch size in Keras
G-2062Upper / lower limit (outlier detection)The two cut-offs of the z-score method, μ−3σ and μ+3σ; a value below the lower limit or above the upper limit counts as an outlier.Note ML-041Z-score outlier method
G-2063Upsampling (resampling by weight)Drawing a new dataset of the same size in which each row is picked with probability equal to its weight, so heavily weighted rows appear more often for the next model.Note ML-110AdaBoost
G-2064User-AgentA short text a browser sends with each request to say what it is; some servers refuse requests without one, so scraping code sends one too.Note ML-014CSV files
G-2065UTF-8The most common text encoding (the rulebook that maps characters to bytes); it covers almost every character in every language and is read_csv’s default.Note ML-014CSV files
G-2067Validation setData held back from training to check and tune a model before the final test.Note DL-011Training curves (History)
G-2066Validation set (blending)In blending, a part of the training data set aside before the base models are trained; the base models predict on it, and the meta-model is trained on those predictions.Note ML-121Stacking and blending
G-2068ValueIn self-attention, the vector each word contributes to the weighted sum that becomes a word’s new vector; it comes from the word’s embedding through a learned value matrix.Note DL-074Self-attention (query, key, value)
G-2069Vanilla gradient descentAnother name for batch gradient descent, the plain version, which uses the whole training set for every weight update.Note DL-020Batch gradient descent
G-2070Vanishing gradientGradients shrinking towards 0 as they pass through many layers, which slows learning.Note DL-018Vanishing gradient
G-2071VariableOne column of a dataset.Note ML-019Features
G-2072Variable-length many-to-manyA sequence-to-sequence setup (many-to-many) whose output length can differ from its input length.Note DL-058Types of RNN (many-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many)
G-2073Variance (of a model)How much a model’s predictions change when it is trained on a different sample of the data; a different meaning from the variance of a column.Note ML-061Bias-variance trade-off
G-2074Variance (of data)The average squared distance of the values from their mean; the square of the standard deviation; divide by n for a population (NumPy default) or n−1 for a sample (pandas default).Note ML-046Variance
G-2228Variance around a point vThe average squared distance of the values to v; smallest when v is the sample mean.Note MA-006Variance
G-2075Variance inflation factor (VIF)A number for each input column that shows how well the other inputs predict it, 1/(1−Rj2​); above 5 signals multicollinearity (the input is redundant).Note ML-055Multicollinearity
G-2076Variance of a random variableHow spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, Var(X)=E[(X−E[X])2].Note MA-012Expected value and variance of a random variable
G-2077Variance reductionThe drop in mean squared error from a node to its children; a regression tree uses it to compare splits, as a classification tree uses information gain.Note ML-093Regression trees
G-2081VectorA list of numbers: a 1D tensor.Note ML-010Vectors and feature vectors
G-2079Vector (geometric view)A point in a coordinate system, drawn as an arrow from the origin.Note MA-048Vectors and feature vectors
G-2080Vector additionAdding matching components; geometrically, placing the second arrow’s tail at the first arrow’s tip.Note MA-052Linear combinations, span and basis
G-2082Vector-valued functionA function that takes several numbers in and gives several numbers out, f:Rn→Rm; we read it as a stack of m ordinary functions.Note MA-063Jacobian and matrix gradients
G-2083Vectorisation (of code)Writing a computation as operations on whole arrays instead of Python loops, which runs much faster.Note ML-057Batch gradient descent
G-2084Vectorization (of data)Converting data such as text into vectors of numbers, because ML algorithms work only with numbers.Note ML-010Tensors
G-2085Velocity vThe direction and size of the current move, built from past gradients: vt​=βvt−1​+η∇L(wt​).Note DL-034SGD with momentum
G-2086Venn diagramA picture of events as circles inside a rectangle; overlaps show shared outcomes.Note MA-013Venn diagrams and contingency tables
G-2087verbosescikit-learn setting that prints progress messages during training.Note ML-100Bagging
G-2258VertexA corner of the feasible region; a linear program always has a best point at a vertex.Note MA-068Linear and quadratic programming
G-2088VGG16An image-recognition network (a CNN) of 13 convolution layers (all 3 × 3) in 5 blocks plus 3 dense layers, trained on ImageNet.Note DL-052Visualising what a CNN learns
G-2089View Page SourceBrowser option that shows a page’s raw HTML.Note ML-017Web scraping
G-2090Virtual environmentA separate folder with its own copy of Python and its own packages, one per project, so the projects’ package versions do not clash.Note ML-011Setup: conda, Jupyter and Colab
G-2091Vision Transformer (ViT)A transformer that reads an image as a sequence of small patches.Note DL-071Transformer
G-2092Vocabulary (V)The list of distinct words (tokens) in a set of texts; in a translation model, those of the target language, with one output node per word.Note DL-084Transformer decoder
G-2094VolatileChanging quickly and unpredictably.Note MA-028Kurtosis and moments
G-2095Voting classifierA classifier that combines several trained classifiers by voting.Note ML-097Voting ensembles
G-2096Voting ensembleSeveral models trained on the same data, combined by majority vote (classification) or mean (regression).Note ML-096Voting ensembles
G-2097Voting regressorA regressor that predicts the mean (or weighted mean) of several trained regressors’ predictions.Note ML-098Voting ensembles
G-2098Vowpal WabbitA fast learning library that can learn from data a piece at a time as it arrives (online learning).Note ML-005Online learning
G-2099Ward linkageA rule for the distance between two clusters in hierarchical clustering: how much the total squared distance to the centroids grows if the two are merged.Note ML-125Hierarchical clustering
G-2100warm_startSetting that keeps already-trained trees and adds new ones on the next fit.Note ML-105Random forest
G-2101Wayback MachineA web archive that keeps copies of web pages as they were.Note ML-017Web scraping
G-2102WCSS (inertia)Within-cluster sum of squares: the sum of squared distances from each point to its own centroid; a smaller value means tighter clusters.Note ML-122Elbow method and WCSS
G-2103Weak dualityEvery value of the related helper (dual) function is at most the true minimum of the original (primal) problem, so any dual value is a floor (lower bound) on the best answer.Note MA-066Lagrange multipliers, KKT and duality
G-2104Weak learnerA model whose accuracy is only a little better than random guessing.Note ML-109Boosting
G-2105Web scrapingWriting code that extracts data from web pages.Note ML-017Web scraping
G-2106Weight (in a network)A number the network learns on the connection between two neurons; it sets how strongly one neuron’s output counts in the next neuron’s sum.Note DL-004Perceptron
G-2111Weight (in a weighted mean)A number saying how much a value counts in a weighted mean.Note MA-005Measures of central tendency
G-2108Weight decayAnother name for the L2 penalty: each gradient step shrinks the coefficients by a fixed factor.Note ML-064Ridge regression
G-2107Weight decay factorThe number 1−ηλ, a little below 1, by which L2 regularisation multiplies every weight at each update, so the weights shrink a little every step.Note DL-026L1 and L2 regularisation in neural networks
G-2109Weight matrix (Wk)All weights entering layer k: one row per node of layer k−1, one column per node of layer k.Note DL-010Forward propagation
G-2110Weight updateThe AdaBoost step that raises the weights of misclassified rows (times eα) and lowers the rest (times e−α), so the next model pays more attention to the mistakes.Note ML-110AdaBoost
G-2112Weight-based algorithmAn algorithm that learns one number per input column from all the points; sensitive to outliers.Note ML-040Outliers
G-2113Weighted averageOne number for a per-class score: the mean of the score over classes, each class counted by how many items really belong to it (its support).Note ML-076Precision, recall and F1
G-2114Weighted errorThe total sample weight of the rows a model misclassifies; AdaBoost uses it to judge how good that model is.Note ML-110AdaBoost
G-2115Weighted impurity decreaseHow much a split lowers the impurity, weighted by the share of rows that reach the node; trees use it to judge splits (the Δ of min_impurity_decrease) and to score feature importance.Note ML-108Feature importance
G-2116Weighted input (zk)The numbers a layer computes before its activation: each node’s weighted sum of the previous layer’s outputs plus its bias, zk=WkTak−1+bk.Note DL-010Forward propagation
G-2117Weighted meanA mean in which each value is multiplied by a weight saying how much it counts.Note MA-005Measures of central tendency
G-2118Weighted quantile sketchXGBoost’s method for choosing candidate split points in a column: it places bin edges at quantiles in which each row counts by its Hessian (weighted quantiles).Note ML-117XGBoost
G-2119Weighted sumIn self-attention, the value vectors multiplied by their weights and added together; the result is the word’s new, context-aware vector.Note DL-076Self-attention (query, key, value)
G-2120weightsVotingClassifier and VotingRegressor setting that gives each base model’s vote a different importance.Note ML-097Voting ensembles
G-2121Welch’s ANOVAA version of ANOVA that works even when the groups’ spreads differ (it does not assume equal variances).Note MA-046One-way ANOVA
G-2122Welch’s t-testThe two-sample t-test that works even when the two groups’ spreads differ (it does not assume equal variances).Note MA-043T-tests: one-sample, two-sample, paired
G-2181WhiskerThe line in a box plot from the box to the last value inside the fence; it shows how far the ordinary values reach, and values beyond it are drawn as separate dots.Note ML-019Percentiles, quartiles and box plots
G-2123WinsorizationHandling outliers by capping them at percentile limits: values beyond a chosen low or high percentile are replaced by that percentile’s value.Note ML-043Capping (winsorization)
G-2124Wisdom of the crowdThe combined judgement of many is often more accurate than any one member’s.Note ML-095Ensemble learning
G-2125With replacementSampling in which each drawn item is put back, so it can be drawn again.Note ML-099Bagging
G-2126Without replacementDrawing items without putting them back, so later draws depend on earlier ones.Note MA-010Independent and mutually exclusive events
G-2127Word embeddingA learned real-valued vector for each word; words used in similar ways get nearby vectors.Note DL-057Word embeddings
G-2128WordNetAn English dictionary that arranges words from general to specific; ImageNet’s categories follow it.Note DL-051Pretrained models and ImageNet
G-2129X, yUsual names for the input table and the output column.Note ML-010Tensors
G-2130XAMPPA free package that runs a web server and a MySQL server on one computer.Note ML-015JSON and SQL data
G-2131Xavier (Glorot) normalStarting weights drawn from a normal distribution whose spread is set by the layer’s size, standard deviation 1/fan-in​ or 2/(fan-in+fan-out)​, so the signal keeps its size from layer to layer.Note DL-030Xavier and He initialisation
G-2132Xavier (Glorot) uniformStarting weights drawn evenly between ±6/(fan-in+fan-out)​, a range set by the layer’s size, so the signal keeps its size from layer to layer.Note DL-030Xavier and He initialisation
G-2133XGBoosteXtreme Gradient Boosting: a library that implements gradient boosting with many speed and accuracy optimisations.Note ML-117XGBoost
G-2134XORThe logic function that outputs 1 when exactly one of two inputs is 1.Note DL-003Problem with the perceptron (XOR)
G-2135Yates’ continuity correctionA small adjustment to χ2 for 2 by 2 tables, applied by default in chi2_contingency.Note MA-045Chi-square tests
G-2136Yeo-Johnson transformA power transform that makes a column closer to normal, like Box-Cox but also working on zero and negative values; scikit-learn’s default.Note ML-030Power transformer
G-2137Z statisticThe number a z-test computes from the sample: how many standard errors the sample mean lies from the mean claimed by H0​.Note MA-039Z-test and rejection regions
G-2138Z-procedureThe way to build a confidence interval for a mean when the population standard deviation σ is known: xˉ±zα/2​σ/n​.Note MA-035Confidence intervals
G-2141Z-scoreA value after standardization: how many standard deviations it lies from the mean.Note ML-041Z-score outlier method
G-2139Z-score methodOutlier detection that flags values more than 3 standard deviations from the mean; for roughly normal columns.Note ML-041Z-score outlier method
G-2140Z-score normalizationAnother name for standardization: rescaling a column so each value becomes its z-score, how many standard deviations it lies from the mean.Note ML-023Standardization
G-2142Z-tableA table that gives, for many values of z, the probability that a standard normal value falls below z, written Φ(z); used to find normal probabilities.Note MA-025Standard normal and the z-table
G-2143Z-test (one-sample)A test of whether a population’s mean equals a claimed value μ0​, used when the population spread σ is known and Xˉ is normal: z=(xˉ−μ0​)/(σ/n​).Note MA-039Z-test and rejection regions
G-2144Zero initialisationStarting every weight (and bias) at 0; with ReLU or tanh nothing trains.Note DL-029Weight initialisation
G-2146Zero padding (image)Adding rows and columns of 0-valued pixels around an image, so a convolution’s feature map can keep the image’s size.Note DL-043Padding and strides
G-2145Zero padding (text)Adding all-zero word vectors to shorter texts so that every text has the same length.Note DL-055Sequence padding
G-2147Zero-ablationSetting a part’s output to 0 and running the rest of the model unchanged, to see what that part does.Note DL-089MLP blocks as fact storage
G-2148Zero-centred activationAn activation whose outputs average about 0 over a layer, positive and negative; it feeds the next layer roughly centred inputs, which helps training converge faster.Note DL-027Activation functions
G-2149Zero-frequency problemA probability of 0 for a value never seen with a class, which forces that class’s score to 0.Note ML-083Naive Bayes
G-2150λ (lambda), alphaThe strength of the regularisation penalty; alpha in scikit-learn.Note ML-062Regularisation
